Name: oracle_transfer_gap_steering
Title: Steering to the Judge, Not the Property: Does Interpretable-Feature Control of Scientific Designs Survive a Change of Oracle?
Short Hypothesis: Interpretable-feature steering produces property gains that are partly an artifact of the specific in-silico oracle used to guide/evaluate it: a large fraction of the measured gain evaporates when the SAME steered objects are scored by an independent, more trustworthy oracle. This oracle-transfer gap is a new evaluation axis for steering -- cross-oracle transfer rather than single-oracle gain -- and a steering-specific form of judge overfitting distinct from classic reward hacking: the generator overfits whatever in-silico judge scored it, on de-novo scientific designs rather than a learned reward model in an RL loop. We hypothesize the gap is systematic (worse at higher steering strength, worse for oracles that share representational features with the steered model), and that a cheap, intervention-free internal signature -- the alignment of the steering direction with oracle-agnostic physicochemical features versus oracle-specific idiosyncrasy -- predicts which steers transfer across oracles. Primary pre-registered endpoint: the transfer gap for one property (logP) in one domain (molecules), above natural-object inter-oracle disagreement.
Related Work: Text-LLM steering studies establish that steering is fragile and trades off with capability (Mind the Performance Gap 2026; The Rogue Scalpel 2025; 'When the Coffee Feature Activates on Coffins' 2026), that interpretability weakly predicts steering utility (Does Higher Interpretability Imply Better Utility 2025), and that steering reliability has geometric predictors (Understanding Unreliability of Steering Vectors 2026). Scientific interpretability-of-generation work (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; chemistry-LM SAEs 2025) reports property GAINS measured by a single in-silico oracle and never asks whether those gains are oracle-dependent artifacts. Sim-to-real work (Intervention Design for Sim2Real 2020; SourceNet 2026) studies train/deploy domain gaps for predictors, not steering-of-generators. My own prior proposals each audit one property class against one better oracle; NONE isolates the general, cross-domain phenomenon that a steering-induced gain is contingent on the CHOICE of measuring oracle, quantifies how much survives an oracle swap, or identifies an internal signature predicting oracle-robustness. This reframes steering reliability as a MEASUREMENT-TRANSFER problem: the danger is not overshoot but that the model steers toward the quirks of whatever judge scored it. This is a steering-specific analogue of reward hacking, but the overfit target is a fixed measurement oracle applied to de-novo designs -- not a learned reward model in an RL loop -- and the failure is diagnosed by an oracle SWAP rather than reward-model probing. If the gap is real, evaluation protocols for molecular/protein steering should become multi-oracle by default, and a cheap internal robustness signature enables pre-screening steer directions before expensive high-fidelity or wet-lab evaluation. Audience: interpretability, generative molecular/protein design, and surrogate-model evaluation communities.
Abstract: Interpretable-feature steering is judged almost universally by one number: an in-silico oracle says the target property increased. But scientific properties are measured by many imperfect instruments, and a control method that genuinely changed the property should look good to any competent judge. We test whether steering-induced gains are robust to a change of oracle, or whether steering silently optimizes the idiosyncrasies of the specific judge that guided it -- an oracle-transfer gap, a steering-specific form of judge overfitting distinct from classic reward hacking. Using ESM-2 protein language models and a SMILES chemical language model with sparse autoencoders, we steer property-linked features and score the SAME steered objects with multiple independent oracles per property (e.g., for logP: distinct empirical estimators; for stability: a learned head vs a physics-based estimator; for structure content: DSSP-on-ESMFold vs an alternative predictor). We (1) quantify the oracle-transfer gap = fraction of the guiding-oracle gain that vanishes under an independent oracle, and its dose-response with steering strength; (2) test whether the gap is larger when the guiding oracle shares features with the steered model than for a physics-based judge; (3) LOCATE an intervention-free robustness signature -- projection of the steering direction onto oracle-agnostic vs oracle-specific features -- that predicts per-steer transfer; and (4) deploy a consensus-orthogonalized steering controller that keeps only oracle-invariant gains. Our primary contribution is the phenomenon; the predictor and the mitigation are secondary. If the gap is real, molecular/protein steering evaluation should become multi-oracle by default, and the predictor enables pre-screening steers before costly high-fidelity or wet-lab checks -- of direct use to the interpretability, generative-design, and surrogate-evaluation communities.
Experiments:
Shared setup (fixed once, reused below). MODELS (frozen): ESM-2 150M and 650M (public checkpoints); a GPT-style SMILES chemical LM (~85M params, MOSES-trained or equivalent public checkpoint). Frozen; only SAEs/probes trainable. SAEs: TopK and Ordered/Matryoshka on the residual stream at an intrinsic-dimension-chosen layer (plus a second layer), width 16x, k=32, Adam lr 1e-3, ~40M activation tokens, seeds {0,1,2}; reconstruction accepted at fraction-variance-unexplained <=0.2. ORACLE PANELS (>=3 independent oracles per target property, each measuring the same physical quantity by different means): molecules -- logP via Crippen/RDKit vs an ML logP model vs a group-contribution estimator; size via exact MW vs a learned descriptor; polarity via TPSA vs an empirical solubility model. Proteins -- hydrophobicity via GRAVY vs a learned head; secondary-structure content via DSSP-on-ESMFold vs an alternative structure predictor; stability via a fine-tuned ML head vs a physics-based (FoldX/Rosetta-style) estimator. Each oracle is pre-labeled "model-adjacent" (learned, may share features with the LM's training signal) or "physics-based" (mechanistic, independent). PRECONDITION: report inter-oracle agreement on ~2,000 NATURAL held-out objects per domain first, to bound the gap expected from oracle noise alone, and report pairwise oracle correlations so gaps are read relative to oracle independence. PRE-REGISTERED PRIMARY ENDPOINT: the transfer gap on ONE primary property (molecular logP) in ONE primary domain (SMILES LM), above natural-object inter-oracle disagreement; all other properties/domains are secondary/confirmatory. Oracle independence is measured as pairwise oracle correlation on natural objects; a panel whose members correlate > 0.9 is too dependent to support a transfer-gap claim for that property. VALIDITY gates: RDKit-validity + SA (molecules), ESMFold pLDDT + pseudo-perplexity (proteins); core analysis restricted to valid objects. FEATURE BANK: ~30-50 property-linked SAE features per domain, selected by concept-correlation / probe AUROC against the panel-AVERAGE (not one oracle), plus difference-of-means baselines. Compute: two ESM-2 sizes + small SMILES LM + lightweight oracle models on 1-2 GPUs, academic-feasible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- steering gains partly evaporate under an independent oracle: the oracle-transfer gap exists): Tests that a large fraction of measured gain does not transfer to held-out oracles scoring the SAME objects. Design: for each feature designate one panel member as the GUIDING oracle (rotated across members to avoid single-oracle idiosyncrasy), sweep steering strength (6 levels), generate 200 objects per level, and score every object under the guiding oracle AND every held-out panel oracle. Decisive metric first: ORACLE-TRANSFER GAP = 1 - (mean held-out-oracle gain)/(guiding-oracle gain); then SILENT-OVERCLAIM RATE = fraction of steers judged successful by the guiding oracle but not by the panel majority. Baseline to subtract: the gap expected from natural-object inter-oracle disagreement (precondition). Convincing: mean transfer gap >= 0.3 above the natural-object baseline, and silent-overclaim rate >= 0.2, with matched-non-property-feature and random-direction controls near 0. Valid-object rates are matched across strengths/conditions (reported, and reweighted if they differ) so the gap is not a filtering artifact. Undecidable band: transfer gap in [0.1, 0.3) above baseline OR silent-overclaim in [0.1, 0.2) -> gap present but modest; report magnitude, do not headline. Negative result (gap < 0.1 above baseline): gains transfer cleanly -- a valuable positive result that interpretable steering targets genuine physics, not judge idiosyncrasy.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- the gap is systematic: it grows with steering strength): Tests the dose-response of the gap. Uses Experiment 1's strength sweep. Decisive metric first: slope of transfer gap vs steering strength (per-feature, mixed-effects, CIs), then whether the SILENT-OVERCLAIM RATE rises with strength. Convincing: positive slope with CI excluding 0 for a majority of features, gap at the highest strength >= 1.5x the gap at the lowest. Undecidable band: slope CI overlapping 0 but point estimate positive, or high/low ratio in [1.1, 1.5) -> weak dose-dependence; report. Negative result (flat or negative slope): the gap is strength-independent -- refines H1 (a fixed oracle bias rather than optimization-driven overfitting).

Experiment 3 (H3 -- the gap is worse when guiding with a model-adjacent oracle than a physics-based one): Tests the feature-leakage prediction. Systems compared: guiding with model-adjacent vs physics-based panel members, at matched steering budget. Decisive metric first: difference in transfer gap between the two guiding-oracle classes (mixed-effects effect size, CIs). Also show the blind spot: correlation between validity/pseudo-perplexity/guiding-oracle confidence and the true transfer gap (hypothesis |r| <= 0.2). Convincing: model-adjacent gap exceeds physics-based gap by effect size d >= 0.5 with CI excluding 0, and blind-spot |r| <= 0.2. Undecidable band: d in [0.1, 0.3) or blind-spot |r| in [0.2, 0.4) -> weak leakage effect; report. Negative result (d < 0.1): the gap is not larger for model-adjacent oracles -- the feature-leakage mechanism is unsupported, reported honestly.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- an intervention-free oracle-agnostic-alignment signature predicts which steers transfer): Tests the predictor. For each steering direction compute (a) projection onto an ORACLE-AGNOSTIC subspace (features predicting the property consistently across ALL panel oracles) vs ORACLE-SPECIFIC directions (predicting only the guiding oracle's residual after removing panel consensus), (b) decoder-direction overlap, (c) concept-correlation. Decisive metric first: Spearman rho / out-of-sample R^2 of per-steer transfer gap regressed on oracle-agnostic-alignment, compared against a concept-correlation baseline; then precision@k for selecting oracle-robust steers as a pre-flight filter, then compute saved by skipping non-transferring steers before running the full panel. Convincing: oracle-agnostic-alignment reaches |rho| >= 0.5 and adds >= 0.1 R^2 over concept-correlation, precision@10 >= 0.7. NULL MODEL: refit the regressor on permuted (steer, gap) pairs and on random directions -- the oracle-agnostic-alignment predictor must beat both. CALIBRATION: report ECE of the pre-flight transfer classifier, not only rank correlation. Undecidable band: |rho| in [0.2, 0.4) or added-R^2 in [0.03, 0.1) -> weak predictor; report, withhold the pre-flight claim. Negative result (|rho| < 0.2, added-R^2 < 0.03): the internal signature does not predict transfer -- the predictor contribution is withdrawn, leaving the phenomenon (Experiment 1) as the result.

Experiment 5 (mitigation -- consensus-aligned steering keeps robust gain): Tests whether steering along the oracle-CONSENSUS subspace (or gating out low-agnostic-alignment steers) Pareto-dominates naive single-oracle steering. Systems compared: consensus-aligned vs naive steering on a gain-vs-transfer frontier. Decisive metric first: consensus (panel-majority) property gain retained at matched validity, then transfer gap, then novelty/diversity. Convincing: consensus-aligned steering retains >= 70% of naive robust gain while cutting the transfer gap by >= 30% at matched validity (Pareto improvement). Undecidable band: robust-gain retention in [50%, 70%) or gap reduction in [10%, 30%) -> partial improvement; report the frontier. Negative result: consensus steering loses > half the robust gain or does not shrink the gap -- no free mitigation; report the tradeoff.

Experiment 6 (robustness of H1-H4): Repeat across both domains, both ESM-2 sizes, TopK vs Ordered SAEs, two layers, and all target properties; report which properties show the largest transfer gaps and the fraction of cells where the gap, its dose-response, the model-adjacent effect, and the predictor replicate. Also report sensitivity to panel size (drop one oracle, re-estimate the consensus). A finding stable in <50% of cells is reported as property-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) All oracles are in-silico; the claim is deliberately about ROBUSTNESS ACROSS INDEPENDENT JUDGES, not wet-lab truth—but a gain that fails to transfer across competent oracles is prima facie untrustworthy, and a physics-based panel member reduces circularity. We report the panel's inter-oracle agreement on NATURAL objects first to bound expected gap from oracle noise alone. 2) Some panel oracles may themselves be biased/correlated, shrinking apparent gaps; we choose maximally mechanistically-distinct oracles and report their pairwise correlation so the gap is interpreted relative to oracle independence. 3) The transfer gap could partly reflect validity collapse rather than oracle-specific optimization; we restrict core analysis to valid objects and report the gap separately. 4) The robustness predictor may be property- or model-specific; we test multiple properties, sizes, and SAE variants and report where it fails. 5) Defining the 'oracle-agnostic subspace' depends on the panel; a richer panel gives a cleaner consensus—we quantify sensitivity to panel size. 6) SAE quality/layer choice could confound; controlled with TopK and Ordered SAEs, multiple layers, difference-of-means baselines, and random-direction controls. 7) If gains transfer cleanly across oracles (small gap), that is a valuable positive result establishing that interpretable-feature steering targets genuine physics rather than judge idiosyncrasy.

Name: hazard_entanglement_asymmetry
Title: Easy to Arm, Hard to Disarm: An Entanglement Asymmetry Between Hazardous and Benign Design Features in Scientific Generative Models
Short Hypothesis: In molecular and protein generative models, interpretable features exhibit a dual-use entanglement asymmetry: hazardous structural properties (toxicophores, known toxin/venom motifs, reactive groups) can be AMPLIFIED cheaply by steering ostensibly-benign, property-labeled features, yet cannot be SUPPRESSED without disproportionate collateral loss of valid, benign design capability. We hypothesize this asymmetry mirrors the capability/safety entanglement documented in text LLMs but is sharper and objectively measurable here because hazard is a verifiable structural fact, and that the degree of asymmetry is predicted by how much a hazard shares its feature subspace with benign design features.
Related Work: SAE-based safety steering is well developed in TEXT LLMs: refusal steering (Steering Language Model Refusal with SAEs, 2024) and detoxification (Breaking Bad Tokens, 2025; GSAE, 2025; Safe-SAIL, 2025) all report that suppressing an unsafe concept degrades general capability, revealing deep entanglement between safety-relevant and general features. Separately, scientific-model interpretability (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; pathology-FM SAEs 2024; chemistry-LM SAEs 2025) discovers and steers interpretable features toward single BENIGN target properties, treating hazard only implicitly. The 'Guiding Generative Models for Protein Design' review (2025) notes models undersample rare regions but does not study hazard controllability. No prior work (a) transfers the safety/capability-entanglement phenomenon into SCIENTIFIC generative models where hazard is a structurally-verifiable fact (RDKit SMARTS toxicophores, HMMER toxin motifs) rather than fuzzy text behavior, (b) tests a DIRECTIONAL ASYMMETRY between cheap hazard amplification and costly hazard suppression, or (c) ties that asymmetry to feature-subspace overlap between hazard and benign design. This distinguishes us from my prior 'intervention-leakage' proposal (which asks whether a single-feature suppression leaks through alternative decoding routes) by instead measuring the amplify-vs-suppress cost asymmetry and its collateral impact on legitimate design capability. It converts a known text-LLM tension into an auditable, high-stakes dual-use risk metric for scientific design. We separate the novelty axes explicitly: NEW SETTING (structurally-verifiable hazard oracles replacing fuzzy text behavior) versus NEW MECHANISM (subspace-overlap prediction of the asymmetry). Three testable novelty-bearing claims: (H1) benign, property-labeled knobs cheaply amplify hazard; (H2) suppression is disproportionately costly and damages benign design (the Asymmetry Index, our single PRIMARY endpoint); (H3) hazard/benign feature-subspace overlap predicts and can be orthogonalized to lower that cost—a tested hypothesis, not a post-hoc label. Stakeholders who would act on this: biosecurity auditors (certify whether a steering interface can be safely disarmed), model developers (decide when to expose steering), interpretability researchers, and policy teams.
Abstract: Interpretability-guided design promises controllable scientific generation, but control is dual-use: the same interpretable knobs that add a desired property may also arm a model to produce hazardous objects, and safety measures that suppress hazard may cripple legitimate design. Text-LLM studies report that safety-relevant features are entangled with general capability, so suppressing an unsafe concept degrades benign performance. We ask whether this tension transfers, and sharpens, in scientific generative models where hazard is an objective structural fact. We define hazardous properties with hard, non-model evaluators (toxicophore/PAINS/reactive-group SMARTS in molecules; known toxin/venom/cytolytic motifs in proteins) and benign design properties with cheap oracles (logP, QED, secondary-structure content, foldability). Training sparse autoencoders on a SMILES chemical language model and ESM-2, we test a central phenomenon: an entanglement asymmetry in which hazard is cheaply AMPLIFIED by steering ostensibly-benign, property-labeled features (a small steering budget, high validity), but cannot be SUPPRESSED below baseline without a disproportionate drop in valid benign-design capability. Our PRIMARY endpoint is the Asymmetry Index = (cost to suppress)/(cost to amplify); the Collateral Ratio = benign-design loss per unit hazard removed and the subspace-overlap prediction are secondary. We quantify these comparing single-feature, subspace, and difference-of-means interventions and controlling for the known pitfall that SAE-reconstructed steering vectors are unreliable. We then test whether the asymmetry is predicted by the feature-subspace overlap between each hazard and benign design directions. A clean-disarmament (low-asymmetry) result is equally valuable, reported as a positive safety finding. Results give biosecurity auditors and model developers a measurable dual-use risk profile and a practical audit—when to deploy steering, when to avoid it, how to certify a safety intervention.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Models: a GPT-style SMILES chemical LM (a public ~90M-parameter checkpoint pretrained on ChEMBL/ZINC) and ESM-2 at 150M and 650M parameters. All base weights frozen; only SAEs are trained. SAEs: TopK (k=32) and Matryoshka variants, dictionary 16384, trained on 200M residual-stream activations at a mid layer (60% depth), seeds {0,1}, FVU reported. HAZARD properties, hard non-model evaluators: molecules -- toxicophore/PAINS SMARTS and reactive/electrophilic-group and structural-alert counts via RDKit (10 alert classes); proteins -- known toxin/venom/cytolytic motifs via HMMER against curated toxin HMMs plus regex (8 motif classes). BENIGN design properties, cheap oracles: molecules -- logP band, QED, ring/scaffold target, synthetic accessibility (SA); proteins -- alpha-helix/beta-sheet fraction (DSSP on ESMFold), GRAVY, a fold/foldability target. VALIDITY gates: RDKit-validity + SA<=6 for molecules; ESMFold pLDDT>=0.6 + pseudo-perplexity within 1.5x baseline for proteins. Steering budget = L2 norm of the added intervention vector, in units of the mean residual-stream norm at the site (so "0.5" = half the typical activation norm); all costs reported in these normalized budget units. Every intervention uses SAE decoder directions and difference-of-means directions DIRECTLY (never SAE re-encodings of steering vectors, the documented OOD/sign pitfall), with a norm-matched random-direction control. 18 hazard/motif classes total across domains; 500 generations per condition (a class-level bootstrap over 18 classes gives ~80% power to detect an Asymmetry-Index median >= 3 vs the null of 1 at a per-class SD of ~1.5). BASELINES for every direction-based claim: SAE-decoder directions, difference-of-means, supervised linear-probe directions, random norm-matched subspaces, and native property gradients where differentiable. ABLATIONS reported throughout: SAE layer (40/60/80% depth), SAE type (TopK vs Matryoshka), feature-bank construction (probe-AUROC threshold), and the thresholds defining hazard baseline (occurrence) and hazard removed (<5%). Steering is always applied inside the validity gate so a suppression cost cannot be dismissed as generic degeneracy.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Benign knobs cheaply amplify hazard). Tests that steering ostensibly-benign, property-labeled features raises hazard occurrence in finished objects at a small budget. Data/systems: for each of the 18 hazard classes, feature bank of benign property-labeled features (identified by probe AUROC>=0.8 on 2,000 held-out natural objects) vs the hazard's own features; compare amplification via benign features, via hazard features, and via norm-matched random directions. Decisive metric: AMPLIFICATION COST = minimal budget to raise hazard occurrence in valid finished objects from baseline to 50%. Convincing positive: median amplification cost via benign features <= 0.5 budget units (and clearly below the random-direction control, which should need >> 1.0 or never reach 50% within validity). Decision band: cost in (0.5, 1.0] units is MODERATE -- hazard is amplifiable but not "cheap"; we report it as amplifiable-with-effort, not cheap arming. Negative: benign features cannot reach 50% hazard within the validity budget at any tested strength (up to 2.0) means benign knobs do not arm the model, refuting H1 for that class.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- Suppression is disproportionately costly: the asymmetry). Tests that driving hazard below baseline costs far more, and damages benign design, than amplification does. Data/systems: same hazard classes; interventions are single-feature, k-dim subspace (SVD of correlated hazard features), and difference-of-means, each compared to a norm-matched random-direction suppression control. Decisive metric (primary): ASYMMETRY INDEX = suppression cost / amplification cost, where suppression cost = minimal budget to drive baseline hazard occurrence below 5% while holding validity. Secondary: COLLATERAL RATIO = benign-design success loss per unit hazard-occurrence removed, benign-design success = hitting a battery of legitimate targets (logP/QED/scaffold; secondary-structure/fold). Convincing positive: median Asymmetry Index >= 3 (suppression >= 3x costlier than amplification) with Collateral Ratio significantly above the random-direction control (95% bootstrap CI over classes excludes 1x). Decision band: Asymmetry Index in [1.5, 3) is a WEAK asymmetry -- reported as present but modest; in [0.67, 1.5) hazard is essentially as cheap to suppress as to amplify (symmetric). Negative: Asymmetry Index <= 0.67 or Collateral Ratio at/below the random control means hazard can be cleanly disarmed -- a valuable positive safety result reported as refuting the asymmetry.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- Objectively measurable and sharper than the text-LLM analogue). Tests that the entanglement here is quantifiable against a structural ground truth and at least as sharp as the reported text-LLM capability/safety degradation. Data/systems: the Collateral Ratio and validity/diversity curves from Experiment 2, benchmarked against a norm-matched random-direction suppression (the text-LLM-style "generic capability degradation" reference) within the same pipeline. Decisive metric: gap between hazard-suppression Collateral Ratio and the random-direction Collateral Ratio at equal hazard removal, plus the fraction of hazard classes whose ratio exceeds the random reference. Convincing positive: hazard-specific suppression shows Collateral Ratio strictly above random in >= 70% of classes (structured, not generic, entanglement) with every quantity computed from hard structural evaluators (0% reliance on a learned hazard model). Decision band: 50-70% of classes above random is PARTIAL -- entanglement is structured for some hazards only; we enumerate which. Negative: <= 50% (hazard suppression no worse than a random norm-matched edit) means the collateral is generic capability loss, not hazard-specific entanglement, and the "sharper here" claim is withdrawn.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- Subspace overlap predicts the asymmetry). Tests that a hazard's feature-subspace overlap with benign design directions predicts its Asymmetry Index and Collateral Ratio, and that orthogonalized suppression lowers collateral. Data/model: for each hazard class compute subspace overlap with benign directions (mean principal-angle cosine / effective shared rank) from the SAE dictionary; regress Asymmetry Index and Collateral Ratio on overlap (Spearman, bootstrap CI over 18 classes). Mitigation arm: subspace suppression projecting out only the hazard-specific complement (orthogonalized against benign directions) vs plain suppression at equal hazard removal. Decisive metric: Spearman rho between overlap and Asymmetry Index; and Collateral-Ratio reduction from orthogonalized vs plain suppression. Convincing positive: rho >= 0.6 (p<0.05) AND orthogonalized suppression cuts Collateral Ratio by >= 30% at matched hazard removal. Decision band: rho in [0.3, 0.6) means overlap is one factor among several -- reported as partial predictor; orthogonalized-suppression gain in [10%, 30%) is a modest mitigation. Negative: rho <= 0.3 means overlap does not predict the asymmetry (the mechanism claim fails, though the phenomenon from Experiments 1-2 may still stand), and no orthogonalization benefit means the collateral is irreducible in feature space.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Hazard and benign properties are defined by in-silico structural evaluators (RDKit SMARTS, HMMER, ESMFold); these are proxies for real-world hazard/function, so claims concern model-internal, structurally-defined dual-use controllability rather than wet-lab harm. We deliberately study only structural-alert-level hazards with unambiguous detectors and avoid synthesizable-threat detail. 2) The asymmetry could depend on steering budget definition; we sweep budgets and report full amplify/suppress curves rather than single points. 3) SAE quality/layer choice may confound which features 'encode' hazard vs benign; we control with multiple SAE variants, probe verification, difference-of-means directions, and random-direction controls, and we avoid the SAE-reconstructed-steering-vector pitfall documented in the literature. 4) Subspace-overlap predictor may be underpowered with few hazard classes; we include many toxicophore/motif classes across both domains. 5) If no asymmetry is found (hazard is as easy to suppress as amplify, with low collateral), that is a valuable, publishable positive safety result establishing that scientific generative models can be cleanly disarmed. 6) We will responsibly report aggregate metrics and mitigations (orthogonalized suppression), not recipes for producing specific hazardous objects.

Name: steerability_predictor
Title: Decodable but Inert: A Predictive Theory of Which Interpretable Directions Actually Steer Scientific Generative Models
Short Hypothesis: Across biomolecular generative models, whether an interpretable/linearly-decodable direction is causally steerable is NOT random noise but is predicted by cheap, intervention-free geometric quantities computed at the intervention site. Falsifiable core claim: the alignment between the direction and the model's local property-output Jacobian at the intervention layer (how much the downstream computation actually reads that direction) forecasts steering efficacy with higher rank correlation than concept-correlation, probe accuracy, decoder norm, or raw-gradient cosine, across the specified models and sites. This enables a pre-flight test that selects effective steering directions before any generation. If cross-domain generality is weak, we narrow the claim to the smallest family in which it holds.
Related Work: Multiple recent papers independently report the same anomaly: high feature-concept correlation or linear decodability does not guarantee causal steering. The antibody SAE paper (2025) finds TopK SAE features are interpretable but not steerable. The Boltz-1 paper (Jedryszek et al. 2026) finds a beta-strand direction with F1=0.82 that produces zero causal effect. FEGA (Hoang et al. 2026) shows most SAE features lack a stable steering direction and distinguishes value-like vs pointer-like features by their logit-effect geometry. Each treats this as an obstacle or a descriptive taxonomy, and none provides a cheap PREDICTIVE test of steerability nor validates such a predictor as a screening tool across scientific object types. Prior text-LM work on predicting steering utility or side-effects (e.g., SAE-Targeted Steering) targets language attributes and does not use an intervention-free Jacobian-alignment geometry at the biomolecular intervention site. Prior steering work (InterPLM, ProtSAE, FoldSAE, ProtoMech, Matryoshka-SAE) demonstrates steering succeeds for SOME directions but selects them by trial-and-error generation. The concrete problem we target is the expensive generation-based screening of candidate steering directions in scientific design loops. Our proposal turns the shared anomaly into a positive, testable theory and a pre-flight filter, distinct from all prior descriptive or single-direction steering work.
Abstract: A striking anomaly recurs across mechanistic-interpretability studies of scientific generative models: directions that are highly interpretable and linearly decodable frequently produce no causal effect when used to steer generation. Antibody, protein, and structure-prediction studies each independently report this decodable-but-inert phenomenon, yet none explains what distinguishes steerable from inert directions or offers a way to predict steerability before running expensive generation experiments - the bottleneck in direction-based scientific design loops. We propose a predictive theory. Our central hypothesis is that steerability is governed by how strongly the model's downstream computation actually reads a direction at the intervention site, captured by the alignment between the direction and the local property-output Jacobian (the sensitivity of generated properties to activation perturbations). We define a small set of cheap, intervention-free candidate predictors - Jacobian alignment, decoder-direction norm relative to the residual stream, effective read-out via attention/MLP weight projections, raw-gradient cosine, and value-like vs pointer-like effect geometry - and benchmark them against ground-truth steering efficacy measured by property change per unit steer. We evaluate across ESM-2 protein LMs, an antibody LM (p-IgGen), and a SMILES molecular LM, using SAE features and difference-of-means directions, with a pre-registered held-out split so the predictor is never fit per domain. We test whether Jacobian alignment predicts steerability with high rank correlation while concept-correlation and probe accuracy do not, and validate a resulting 'steerability score' as a pre-flight filter that selects effective directions without generation, quantifying generation runs saved. Results would convert a widespread nuisance into an actionable, empirically validated screening principle for controllable scientific design.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Models (three families, all frozen): ESM-2 150M and 650M (masked protein LM), p-IgGen antibody LM (~17M), and a GPT-style SMILES molecular LM (~10M, trained on a ~1.9M-molecule ChEMBL subset or a public checkpoint). Directions bank per model: 40-80 strongly decodable directions - TopK SAE features (and Ordered/Matryoshka where available) with high concept-correlation, plus difference-of-means directions for each measurable property. Properties with cheap evaluators: proteins - alpha-helix/beta-sheet % (DSSP on ESMFold), GRAVY, molecular weight, motifs (HMMER/regex); antibodies - CDR length, net charge, a developability proxy; molecules - logP, QED, ring count, functional-group presence (RDKit SMARTS). GEOMETRY DEFINITION: at a fixed intervention layer L (residual stream), the property-Jacobian J is the gradient of a differentiable property surrogate with respect to the layer-L activation, averaged over a held-out set; Jacobian alignment of a unit direction d is ||proj_d J|| / ||J|| (the fraction of local property sensitivity captured by d), reported at L and swept over 3 candidate layers. Ground-truth steerability of a direction = slope of target-property change per unit steer at low strength, plus the max reliable property gain before validity collapses (validity: pseudo-perplexity/ESMFold pLDDT for proteins, RDKit-validity for molecules); measured over a strength sweep, 5 generation seeds. For non-differentiable evaluators (HMMER, folding) a lightweight differentiable surrogate supplies the Jacobian; surrogate held-out fidelity (R^2/AUROC) is reported. PRE-REGISTRATION: directions and models are split into a fit set (for choosing predictor normalization) and a held-out test set (for all reported rho and precision), fixed before ground-truth steering is measured.

Experiment 1 (H1+H2 - a cheap geometric quantity predicts steerability better than concept-correlation): Tests that causal steerability is non-randomly predicted by intervention-free geometry, and specifically that Jacobian alignment beats concept-correlation/probe accuracy. Decisive metric: Spearman rho between each candidate predictor and ground-truth steerability, with bootstrap CIs, per model and pooled, on the held-out test set. Convincing result: Jacobian alignment attains rho >= 0.5 AND exceeds the concept-correlation/probe-AUROC rho by >= 0.2, with concept-correlation's rho within [-0.2, 0.2] (replicating the "decodable but inert" anomaly). Decision band: Jacobian rho in [0.3, 0.5], or its margin over concept-correlation in [0.1, 0.2] -> suggestive; report as a weak predictor. Negative result (concept-correlation predicts as well as Jacobian alignment) refutes the specific claim; if NO predictor beats rho 0.3, steerability is closer to noise. Controls/baselines compared: effective read-out through downstream attention/MLP input weights, decoder-direction norm relative to typical residual norm, raw-gradient cosine, a value-vs-pointer logit-effect-geometry class, and a random-subspace control; we also report partial correlation controlling for feature strength/decodability so any gain is not a proxy for magnitude.

Experiment 2 (H2 - causal test via synthetic directions): Tests whether Jacobian alignment causes steerability rather than merely correlating. Decisive metric: steerability difference between matched-decodability directions constructed with high vs low Jacobian alignment (low-alignment made by orthogonalizing a decodable direction against the top Jacobian subspace). Convincing result: high-alignment synthetic directions steer (slope > 0 with CI excluding 0) while low-alignment ones are inert (slope indistinguishable from the random-direction control), a monotone effect of alignment across >= 4 alignment levels. Decision band: a monotone trend present but low-alignment directions still steer at >= half the high-alignment slope -> alignment contributes but is not the whole story. Negative result (steerability independent of imposed alignment) refutes the account. We vary intervention layer to check the predictor tracks the layer-dependence of steerability, re-measuring alignment post-construction to confirm the manipulation took.

Experiment 3 (H3 - a pre-flight filter saves screening compute): Tests that ranking directions by the best cheap predictor finds steerable directions without generation-based screening. Decisive metric: precision@10 for actually-steerable directions under the steerability-score ranking. Convincing result: precision@10 >= 0.8, at least 2x the concept-correlation ranking and above random, with generation runs avoided to find 10 good directions >= 50%. Decision band: precision@10 in [0.5, 0.8] -> a useful but imperfect screen. Negative result (precision@10 <= random) refutes H3. Reported per model on the held-out set.

Experiment 4 (H4 - cross-domain generality): Tests whether the predictor's utility holds across protein, antibody, and molecule families. Decisive metric: the Experiment-1 Spearman rho within each family. Convincing result: rho >= 0.4 in all three families. Decision band: rho >= 0.4 in two of three -> partial generality; narrow the headline claim to the families where it holds. Negative result (holds in only one family) means the principle is family-specific, a scientifically informative limit rather than a universal law.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Jacobian alignment requires a differentiable property signal; for properties only measurable by non-differentiable evaluators (HMMER motifs, folding) we substitute a lightweight differentiable surrogate predictor, which may introduce approximation error - we quantify surrogate fidelity and check robustness to surrogate choice. 2) The predictor may be property- or layer-specific rather than universal; we mitigate by testing multiple properties, three layers, and three model families and reporting where it fails, and by narrowing the claim to the supported setting. 3) In-silico steerability and validity are proxies for wet-lab outcomes; claims concern model-internal controllability, not experimental function. 4) The synthetic-direction ablation assumes orthogonalization cleanly removes Jacobian alignment without side effects; we verify by re-measuring alignment post-construction. 5) We present Jacobian alignment as an empirically validated, falsifiable predictor motivated by the intuition that only read directions can causally act - not as a derived theorem; if concept-correlation predicts equally well in some models, the anomaly may be architecture-dependent, which we would still report as informative.

Name: compositional_feature_steering
Title: Do Interpretable Features Compose? A Causal Test of Multi-Constraint Steering in Biomolecular Generative Models
Short Hypothesis: If sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features of protein language models are genuinely disentangled causal handles, then simultaneously steering along several feature directions under a fixed steering budget should compose approximately additively: the joint effect superposes the solo effects, satisfying multiple design constraints at once with low interference and preserved validity, whereas norm-matched raw-activation steering shows destructive interference. We further hypothesize a null: a feature's interpretability score (concept correlation) does NOT predict its compositional steerability, and that low-alpha causal-effect magnitude and decoder-direction geometry do. Ranked by centrality, the contributions are: (1) the empirical compositionality test, (2) a predictive rule for which features compose, and (3) a geometric orthogonalization fix.
Related Work: A rapidly growing body of work applies sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to protein language models for single-property steering: InterPLM, ProtSAE, FoldSAE (RFdiffusion), MotifAE, ProtoMech (cross-layer transcoders), and antibody/RNA SAEs. Critically, every one of these steers toward ONE target property (e.g., a zinc-finger motif, thermostability) and evaluates only whether that single property appears; none report joint success under two or more simultaneous constraints, none quantify cross-feature interference, and none provide a predictor of which features can be combined. The antibody SAE paper (2025) reports the crucial anomaly that high feature-concept correlation does NOT guarantee causal steerability, but does not explain what does, nor study multi-property control. Our proposal is the first to systematically test COMPOSITIONALITY: whether independently identified feature directions can be combined to satisfy multiple constraints simultaneously, and to turn that incidental anomaly into a testable, generalizable predictor. This matters because real design workflows (enzyme engineering, antibody optimization, de novo scaffolds) routinely require several constraints at once (fold AND stability AND a functional motif AND localization), so single-property steerability does not establish practical controllability.
Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can decompose protein language model (pLM) activations into human-interpretable features, and recent work shows individual features can steer generation toward single target properties. Real biomolecular design, however, requires satisfying multiple constraints at once (e.g., a specific fold AND high thermostability AND a binding motif AND a localization signal). We ask a simple, falsifiable question: do interpretable features COMPOSE? If features are truly disentangled causal handles, steering along several feature directions simultaneously under a fixed budget should approximately superpose their individual effects, hitting multiple targets with little interference and preserved sequence validity. We test this on ESM-2 with SAEs trained on its residual stream, defining an Interference Score (degradation of each property when co-steered versus solo) and a Validity Budget (steering strength before sequences become non-viable, measured by pseudo-perplexity, ESMFold pLDDT, and property predictors). Across pre-registered pairs and triples of properties (secondary-structure content, thermostability proxy, hydrophobicity/GRAVY, catalytic-site motifs), we compare SAE-feature steering against norm-matched raw-activation, random, PCA, and top-activation baselines, and against orthogonalized-feature steering. We then test whether interpretability score predicts compositional steerability, and whether low-alpha causal-effect magnitude and decoder geometry predict it instead. We expect SAE features to compose more gracefully than raw steering but to exhibit systematic interference clusters, and that steerability is predicted by causal-effect magnitude rather than concept correlation. Results yield a practical recipe for multi-constraint design, a rule for selecting compositionally steerable features, and a mechanistic account of when interpretable features act as independent design levers.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP (used by every experiment below). Model: frozen ESM-2 650M (33 layers, hidden width 1280) as primary and frozen ESM-2 150M (30 layers, width 640) as a size-robustness check; both are the public facebook/esm masked protein LMs, weights never updated. Interpretability handles: a TopK sparse autoencoder (SAE; k=32 active latents, dictionary 16,384) trained on residual-stream activations at one layer selected by the intrinsic-dimension elbow (expected near the middle block); a Matryoshka SAE is trained as an architecture-robustness variant. SAE training data: 20M residual-stream token-activations sampled from a 500k-sequence subset of UniRef50 (~60M sequences available; 500k chosen to keep one training run under a day on a single A100); Adam, lr 1e-3, batch 4,096, one training pass, 3 SAE seeds. "Steering" = adding alpha times a unit direction (the SAE decoder column, or a baseline direction) to the chosen layer at all positions during masked-infill generation. Property evaluators (all automated, no wet lab): alpha-helix % and beta-sheet % from DSSP run on ESMFold structures; GRAVY hydrophobicity and molecular weight from Biopython; a thermostability proxy from a ridge head fit on the Meltome Atlas (~48k proteins, held-out R^2 reported); two motifs (C2H2 zinc-finger, Ser-His-Asp catalytic triad) via PROSITE regex/HMMER. FEATURE-SELECTION PROTOCOL (pre-registered to prevent a hand-picked easy-pair benchmark): for each property, features above a fixed concept-correlation floor on 5k held-out UniRef sequences are frozen into a bank BEFORE any co-steering is run; the single best per property gives a ~7-feature bank, expanded to ~30-40 for the regression analyses. All property pairs/triples are enumerated exhaustively (no hand-picking). Generation uses 5 sampling seeds; 200 sequences per condition. All correlations report 95% bootstrap CIs and Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the many pairs/triples.

Experiment 1 (H1 - additive composition of SAE features): Tests whether co-steering several SAE feature directions at once satisfies several constraints simultaneously with minimal interference and preserved validity. Decisive metric: joint success rate = fraction of generated sequences meeting ALL targeted property thresholds at once. Secondary: per-property Interference Score I = (solo gain - co-steered gain)/solo gain. Convincing result: joint success >= 0.6x the product of the features' solo success rates AND mean I <= 0.2 while the fraction of foldable sequences (ESMFold pLDDT >= 70) falls by < 10 points versus solo steering. Decision band (indeterminate): mean I in [0.2, 0.4] OR joint success in [0.4, 0.6]x the product -> report "partial composition," which neither confirms additive composition nor the destructive alternative, and defer the verdict to the geometric analysis in Experiment 4. Negative result (mean I > 0.4 or joint success < 0.4x product) means SAE features do NOT compose additively, refuting H1. Data/systems: all 21 property PAIRS and 10 TRIPLES from the ~7-feature bank, each co-steered at its solo-calibrated alpha (calibrated by a prior per-feature strength sweep recording property gain vs validity). A realistic-design subset couples fold + thermostability + catalytic-triad motif to mirror an enzyme-engineering objective and is reported separately. Robustness: repeat a reduced 3-property protocol on the RiNALMo RNA LM (~650M, frozen) with 2 RNA properties (GC content, a stem-loop motif) to check the compositionality principle transfers across biomolecule type.

Experiment 2 (H2 - raw-activation steering shows destructive interference): Tests the claimed contrast that raw-activation steering interferes where SAE steering does not. Decisive metric: paired difference in mean Interference Score, (raw minus SAE), across the same 21 pairs and 10 triples. Convincing result: norm-matched raw difference-of-means steering (directions matched to each SAE feature's solo property gain and in norm) shows mean I higher by >= 0.15 with a 95% bootstrap CI excluding 0, and lower joint success. Decision band: difference in [0.0, 0.15] -> the two are indistinguishable on interference; report that SAE features offer no compositional advantage over raw steering (a partial refutation of the framing). Negative result (raw I <= SAE I) refutes H2. Systems compared (all norm-matched): (a) additive SAE-feature steering, (b) raw difference-of-means directions, (c) random directions, (d) PCA-of-activations directions, (e) top-activation-token directions, (f) Gram-Schmidt-orthogonalized SAE directions (feeds Experiment 4c).

Experiment 3 (H3 - interpretability score does not predict compositional steerability): Tests whether a feature's concept-correlation predicts how well it composes. Decisive metric: Spearman rho(concept-correlation, compositional steerability), where steerability = 1 - mean I over that feature's pairings. Convincing result for H3 (a null): |rho| <= 0.2 with 95% bootstrap CI contained in [-0.4, 0.4]. Decision band: |rho| in [0.2, 0.4] -> weak, ambiguous predictive value; report as "not clearly predictive." Negative result (rho >= 0.4) means interpretability DOES predict compositional steerability, refuting H3. Data: the ~7-feature bank is small, so we use the pre-registered expanded bank of ~30-40 property-linked features to power this regression, reported with n, CIs, and BH correction.

Experiment 4 (H4 - identifying what does predict it, and a geometric fix): Tests the positive companion to H3: that causal-effect magnitude and decoder geometry predict compositional steerability and that pre-orthogonalization repairs interference. (a) Predictor test - decisive metric Spearman rho(causal-effect magnitude, steerability), where causal magnitude = property change per unit alpha at low alpha; convincing if rho >= 0.5 AND exceeds the concept-correlation rho of Experiment 3 by >= 0.2. (b) Interference geometry - decisive metric rho(|decoder-direction cosine|, pairwise Interference Score) across all feature pairs; convincing if rho >= 0.5. (c) Fix - Gram-Schmidt pre-orthogonalize colliding feature pairs and re-run co-steering; convincing if mean I drops by >= 0.15 absolute with joint success rising and validity retained, while we report the interpretability cost (change in the orthogonalized direction's concept-correlation). Decision band: causal rho in [0.3, 0.5], or geometry rho in [0.3, 0.5], or interference reduction in [0.05, 0.15] -> suggestive but not decisive; report the predictor as a candidate needing more features. Negative result (no predictor beats chance and orthogonalization does not reduce interference) means we fail to identify what governs compositional steerability, so the hypothesis's "we identify what property does" clause is unsupported. Practical payoff: the winning predictor becomes a cheap pre-screen for feature selection, changing steering strategy from "pick the most interpretable feature" to "pick the strongest causal, geometrically non-colliding feature."
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Property evaluators (structure/thermostability predictors) are imperfect proxies for wet-lab truth; conclusions are about in-silico controllability, not experimentally validated function. 2) Compositionality may be trivially poor if all chosen features live in a low-dimensional subspace; we mitigate by selecting features spanning diverse concept types and reporting the full interference matrix. 3) SAE quality and layer choice could confound results; we control by comparing multiple SAE architectures (TopK, Matryoshka) and model sizes, and by steering-magnitude sweeps. 4) The predictive-regression analysis could be underpowered if the feature bank is small; we mitigate by the pre-registered expanded bank of tens of features and report n, CIs, and Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the many pairs/triples. 5) The feature bank and all pairs/triples are frozen before co-steering to prevent cherry-picking of easy pairs. 6) Orthogonalization may reduce interpretability of steered directions, a tradeoff we quantify rather than assume away. 7) The predictor claim is presented as an empirical, falsifiable rule, not a proven mechanistic theory.

Name: physics_field_conservation_steering
Title: Steer the Storm, Break the Balance: Do Interpretable Interventions on Physics-Field Emulators Silently Violate Conservation Laws?
Short Hypothesis: Data-driven physics-field emulators (weather models, fluid/PDE surrogates) hold interpretable, causally-steerable features for LOCAL/phenomenological structures (a cyclone, a vortex, a diffusion front), but do NOT hold a compact, causally-steerable handle on the GLOBAL CONSERVATION LAWS (mass, energy, momentum, and the continuity/divergence constraint) that certify a field as physical. We test this as four falsifiable claims: (H1) local-phenomenon features are causally steerable; (H2) the global conserved integrals are decodable from activations yet NOT preservable by any compact intervention while a local phenomenon is changed; (H3) steering a local feature therefore silently breaks the conserved integrals -- a conservation blind spot that local-plausibility and per-cell validity checks miss but an exact conservation-integral oracle exposes; and (H4) an intervention-free internal conservation-consistency signal flags the violation before rollout. The novelty axis is intervention-level conservation preservation under causal steering in a continuous-field setting -- an evaluation never applied to the physics-steering interventions it targets.
Related Work: Physics Steering (2025) shows a physics foundation model has single directions causally steering vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed; the GraphCast SAE paper (2025) finds interpretable features (cyclones, atmospheric rivers, sea-ice) and shows sparse feature modifications yield physically consistent evolving hurricanes; CFD-surrogate SAE work (2025) extracts monosemantic vorticity/flow features; DIANO and flow-matching-interpretability work embed physics into latent spaces. Crucially, EVERY one of these steers or interprets LOCAL, phenomenological structures and asserts the change looks physically consistent by eyeball or per-region metrics -- NONE verifies that the intervention preserves the GLOBAL conserved integrals (total mass/energy/momentum, or the discrete divergence/continuity constraint) that actually define physical validity. Stated as exact gaps: Physics Steering measured causal steerability of a local direction, not integral preservation; the GraphCast SAE measured local plausibility of the evolved field, not conservation drift; the CFD-surrogate SAE measured feature monosemanticity, not what a feature edit does to global invariants. Separately, conservation-aware ML (physics-informed losses, hard-constraint layers, FlowER for reaction mass balance) treats conservation as an architectural constraint, never asking whether a standard emulator internally represents it or whether interpretable steering respects it. Taxonomy of our contribution: the FINDING is a conservation blind spot in interpretable steering; the MECHANISM is a decodable-but-inert conservation representation; the SETTING is continuous-field emulators with exact integral/differential oracles (not discrete token counting, unlike my prior chemical-atom-balance proposals); the METRIC is intervention-level conservation preservation under causal steering. This is a new evaluation axis, not a re-run of steering: prior work asked can we steer a local phenomenon and does it look consistent, we ask does that steer preserve the global integrals that define physical validity. No prior work (a) tests conservation-law preservation of interpretable-feature interventions on physics-field generators, (b) contrasts local-phenomenon steerability against conservation-law steerability, or (c) provides an internal conservation-consistency audit.
Abstract: The validity of a physical field -- a weather state, a fluid flow, a PDE solution -- is certified not by how realistic any local region looks but by whether it obeys global conservation laws: total mass, energy, and momentum, and the continuity/divergence constraints that follow. Recent interpretability work shows that physics-field emulators (GraphCast-style weather models, fluid/PDE surrogates, physics foundation models) contain interpretable features that can be causally steered to induce or suppress local phenomena such as cyclones and vortices, with changes that look physically consistent. We surface and test a phenomenon these studies never checked: the conservation blind spot. We hypothesize that emulators represent local phenomenology as compact steerable features but do NOT represent the global conservation laws as a steerable handle, so steering a local feature silently breaks the conserved integrals -- a failure invisible to local plausibility and per-cell checks but exposed by exact conservation oracles (grid-integrated mass/energy/momentum and discrete divergence). Using an open weather emulator and a fluid/PDE surrogate with sparse autoencoders on internal activations, we (1) LOCATE candidate local-phenomenon and conservation features; (2) CAUSALLY contrast local-phenomenon control against conservation-preserving control; (3) INTERPRET whether located units encode true global conservation or shallow local proxies; and (4) AUDIT whether an intervention-free conservation-consistency signal flags violating interventions better than local checks. The novelty is a new evaluation axis: intervention-level conservation preservation under causal steering. If it holds, local-plausible steering is insufficient as a validity check and conservation-integral auditing becomes mandatory, telling interpretability, weather, CFD-surrogate, and scientific-foundation-model practitioners when to trust a steered field, reject a feature intervention, or require conservation-aware constraints.
Experiments:
Shared setup (fixed once, reused by every experiment below). MODELS (frozen): (a) a data-driven weather emulator — a FourCastNet-style AFNO model (~70M params) trained on the WeatherBench2 ERA5 subset at 5.625 deg resolution (13 fields: geopotential, temperature, u/v wind, specific humidity, surface pressure); we use the public reproduction checkpoint, no fine-tuning. (b) a fluid/PDE surrogate — a Fourier Neural Operator (~8M params) trained on the PDEBench 2D incompressible Navier-Stokes set (10,000 trajectories provided; we use 8,000 train / 1,000 val / 1,000 test). Both emulators are FROZEN throughout; only SAEs and probes are trainable. SAEs: TopK SAE, dictionary width 16x the activation dimension, k=32, trained on cached activations at one block chosen by an intrinsic-dimension elbow heuristic (also cache a second block for robustness); ~50M spatial-location activation vectors, Adam lr 1e-3, batch 4096, 100k steps, seeds {0,1,2}; we also train an Ordered/Matryoshka SAE with identical budget. Reconstruction is accepted only if the SAE recovers >=0.8 of activation variance (fraction-variance-unexplained <=0.2); below that the layer is rejected before any downstream claim. ORACLES (exact, deterministic on the discrete grid): conservation integrals — total mass/dry-air mass, total energy, total momentum, and the pointwise continuity/divergence residual (mass-flux balance for weather; grid-integrated div(u) for the incompressible surrogate). LOCAL-PHENOMENON oracles: cyclone tracker (vorticity + pressure-minimum), vortex detector (Q-criterion), diffusion-front detector. VALIDITY gates: per-cell physical bounds (non-negative densities, finite values), spectral sanity. Precondition (must pass before any violation claim): confirm unsteered rollouts natively span a range of conserved-integral values and approximately conserve, so "violation" is defined RELATIVE to the unsteered rollout baseline; we report both absolute drift and drift-above-baseline. Compute budget: two frozen emulators + <=4 SAEs on 1-2 GPUs, within an academic lab.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- local phenomenological features ARE causally steerable): Tests the claim that emulators hold interpretable, causally-steerable features for local structures (cyclone, vortex, front). Data: 2,000 held-out test fields per emulator (from the 1,000 NS test trajectories, multiple timesteps; ERA5 held-out dates), used as-is. For each of >=8 local-phenomenon features (identified by concept-correlation / probe AUROC against the local oracle on held-out fields, top directions kept), add/subtract the SAE decoder direction during one forward step across a strength sweep of 6 levels, evolve the field, and measure the DECISIVE metric first: local-phenomenon gain per unit steer (change in cyclone intensity / Q-criterion / front sharpness), with specificity (off-target local change) and a matched-norm random-direction control. Convincing: mean local gain per unit steer with Cohen's d >= 0.8 versus the random-direction control, monotone dose-response (Spearman |rho| >= 0.6) over the sweep, for a majority of the >=8 features in both emulators. Undecidable band: d in [0.2, 0.5) OR |rho| in [0.2, 0.4) -> steerability unestablished for that feature; it is dropped from H2's head-to-head rather than counted either way. Negative result (d < 0.2 across features): local steerability itself fails, the premise for the blind spot collapses, and the study reduces to a controllability audit of physics emulators -- reported as such.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- NO compact, causally-steerable conservation handle exists): Tests that no compact intervention holds a conserved integral fixed while modifying a local phenomenon. Two parts. (2a, decodability floor) Probe SAE features and raw activations to predict each global integral (mass/energy/momentum) and the divergence residual on held-out fields, using partial correlation to remove local-phenomenology confounds; decisive metric: conservation-probe R^2. (2b, steerability) In the SAME pipeline as Experiment 1, attempt to hold each integral fixed while inducing a local change, using four intervention types (TopK SAE feature, Ordered/Matryoshka feature, difference-of-means between high/low-drift fields, activation patching from conserving rollouts); decisive metric: conservation-preserving steering success = fraction of steers that change the local phenomenon (gain d >= 0.8, from Experiment 1's scale) while keeping conserved-integral drift within the unsteered baseline band. Convincing support for H2 (a genuine ABSENCE): integrals are decodable (2a R^2 >= 0.5) yet no intervention type reaches >0.2 conservation-preserving success, and its effect size is <1/3 of local steerability (Experiment 1) -- decodable-but-inert. Undecidable band: 2a R^2 in [0.2, 0.5) leaves decodability itself unresolved (report, do not claim inertness); conservation-preserving success in [0.2, 0.4) means a weak handle may exist -> claim "weak/partial handle", not absence. Negative result for H2 (success >= 0.4 for any intervention, d within 1/3 of local): a compact conservation handle DOES exist -- an equally publishable positive finding enabling conservation-aware steering; report it as refutation of the non-steerability claim. Baseline: compare every interpretable handle against a hard-constraint projection onto the conservation manifold to bound how far interpretable steering is from a guaranteed fix.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- steering a local feature silently breaks global conservation, invisible to local/per-cell checks): Tests the core blind spot. Reuse Experiment 1's local-feature steers; at each strength measure the DECISIVE metric first: SILENT-VIOLATION RATE = fraction of steered fields that are locally-successful (gain d >= 0.8), per-cell-valid, and locally-plausible yet whose conserved-integral drift exceeds the unsteered baseline band. Also report blind-spot magnitude = conserved-integral drift per unit local gain (dose-response), and INVISIBILITY = correlation between local-plausibility/per-cell-validity scores and true conservation drift. Convincing: SILENT-VIOLATION RATE >= 0.3 at the strengths where local steering is judged successful, AND invisibility correlation |r| <= 0.2 (local checks carry essentially no information about conservation drift), with a matched-non-phenomenon-feature control ruling out generic perturbation instability. Undecidable band: SILENT-VIOLATION RATE in [0.1, 0.3) OR invisibility |r| in [0.2, 0.4) -> blind spot present but mild; report magnitude, do not headline. Negative result (rate < 0.1 or |r| > 0.4): local checks already track conservation, so there is no hidden blind spot -- a reassuring positive result that interpretable local steering is conservation-safe.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- an intervention-free internal conservation-consistency signal flags the violation): Tests that a signal read from the steered activation, before rollout, detects conservation-violating steers. Systems compared: internal conservation-probe read-out vs output-side detectors (local plausibility, per-cell validity, spectral sanity) vs a black-box raw-activation probe. Labels come from Experiment 3's oracle-verified violation set. Decisive metric first: detection AUROC of the internal signal for the local-OK/global-broken class, then calibration ECE, then rollout compute saved by rejecting/re-steering before a full multi-step rollout + conservation evaluation. Convincing: internal AUROC >= 0.75 and >= 0.1 absolute above the best output-side detector, ECE <= 0.1. Undecidable band: internal-minus-output-side AUROC gap in [0.0, 0.05] -> the internal signal adds no operational value over cheap output-side checks; report as such. Negative result (internal AUROC < 0.6): no usable internal conservation signal exists; the audit payoff is withdrawn and the contribution narrows to the blind-spot demonstration (Experiment 3).

Experiment 5 (robustness of H2/H3): Repeat Experiments 2-3 across both emulators, TopK vs Ordered SAEs, two layers, and all conserved quantities (mass, energy, momentum, divergence), and test whether single-step conservation error compounds over multi-step rollouts (drift at step 1 vs step 10). Report the subset of (emulator x SAE x quantity) cells where the blind spot and non-steerability replicate (target: majority of cells) versus where they are artifacts; a finding stable in <50% of cells is reported as regime-specific, not general.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Conservation oracles are EXACT for the discrete grid (integrals and divergence are deterministic sums), a strength; the subtlety is that even unsteered emulators do not perfectly conserve, so we define violation RELATIVE to the unsteered rollout baseline and report both absolute and relative drift, restricting strong claims to drift clearly exceeding baseline. 2) The conservation-non-steerability claim is partly an ABSENCE claim; we mitigate by trying multiple intervention types (TopK/Ordered SAE features, difference-of-means, activation patching, conservation-orthogonalized directions), sweeping strength, and head-to-head calibrating that LOCAL features ARE steerable in the same pipeline—so a null conservation result is meaningful, not a weak-model artifact. A positive result (a genuine steerable conservation handle) is equally publishable and directly useful for building conservation-aware emulators without architectural surgery. 3) The blind spot could be confounded with generic instability from any perturbation; random-direction and matched-non-phenomenon-feature controls, plus comparison to the hard-constraint-projection baseline, isolate the conservation-specific effect. 4) Local phenomenology and global conservation are partly entangled (a large local change must draw from somewhere); the controlled dissociation pairs (step 5) and the divergence-residual metric separate 'model knows mass must be conserved locally' from 'model preserves the global integral', and we report where separation is impossible. 5) Requires emulators with accessible internal activations; scope limited to open, instrumentable models (GraphCast-style, FNO/graph CFD surrogates). 6) SAE quality/layer choice could confound Location; controlled with TopK and Ordered SAEs, multiple layers, raw-activation probes, and random-direction controls. 7) An internal conservation probe might not beat a black-box raw-activation probe on raw AUROC; the interpretability diagnosis (local-steerable, conservation-decodable-but-weakly-steerable) and the audit/compute-saving payoff remain the contributions, reported honestly. 8) If steering preserves conservation out of the box, that is a valuable positive result establishing that interpretable interventions on physics emulators are conservation-safe and that these models robustly represent global invariants.

Name: intervention_leak_scientific_design
Title: Does Clamping Fix It? Auditing Whether Interpretable-Feature Interventions Truly Eliminate Undesired Properties in Scientific Generative Models
Short Hypothesis: In safety-critical scientific design, an intervention believed to remove a hazardous property (a toxic substructure, an instability motif, a disallowed fold) frequently fails at the object level: when we clamp/ablate the interpretable feature that encodes it, the model reconstitutes the property through alternative internal routes during iterative/autoregressive decoding. We hypothesize this leakage is substantial, arises SPONTANEOUSLY during ordinary generation (not only under adversarial optimization), and is predicted by concept redundancy - the effective rank of the concept subspace (how many independent SAE directions carry the concept), which is distinct from raw feature count or SAE reconstruction error. A redundancy-aware fix that clamps the whole concept subspace should close the leak.
Related Work: The top-line phenomenon that SAE interventions can be circumvented is not ours: a concurrent text-LLM paper (Cui et al. 2026, 'SAE Interventions are Unreliable: Post-Intervention Recovery') shows clamping an 'unsafe' feature in language models can be optimized around. Our delta is the scientific-object setting and spontaneous leakage. Almost all interpretability-for-design work (InterPLM, ProtSAE, FoldSAE, molecular-transformer SAE circuits, GFlowNet interpretation, chemical-LM steering vector fields, molecular task arithmetic) demonstrates that clamping/steering a feature CHANGES a target property, reporting success at the level of a forward pass or a single generation; dynamic-guardrail and side-effect-prediction work filters or predicts at the output rather than auditing whether the internal suppression itself holds through decoding. No prior work asks whether feature interventions ROBUSTLY eliminate undesired properties in SCIENTIFIC generative models, where 'recovery' is an objectively measurable structural fact rather than fuzzy text behavior, and where multi-step structured decoding (autoregressive SMILES, iterative diffusion denoising) provides many natural re-routing opportunities. We are the first to (i) define and measure intervention leakage for scientific object design, (ii) test whether it arises spontaneously during ordinary generation, and (iii) tie leakage to a pre-specified concept-redundancy metric, yielding a practical audit plus a redundancy-aware multi-feature clamping fix. Adopters: molecular design, protein engineering, and safety/interpretability researchers.
Abstract: Interpretability-guided design increasingly relies on a hopeful assumption: that clamping or ablating an interpretable feature reliably removes the property it encodes - a load-bearing assumption when the property is a safety hazard. We stress-test it for scientific generative models, where 'the property' is an objectively verifiable structural fact: a toxic substructure in a molecule, a destabilizing motif in a protein, or a disallowed fold. We define intervention leakage as the rate at which a suppressed, undesirable property reappears in the FINAL generated object despite an active feature-level intervention, and ask how often an intervention thought to remove a hazardous motif still yields a dangerous final candidate. Using autoregressive SMILES chemical LMs and ESM-2 protein LMs with sparse autoencoders, we clamp features a forward-pass analysis identifies as encoding a target undesired property, run ordinary iterative generation, and check finished objects with hard structural evaluators (RDKit substructure matching, HMMER/regex motifs, DSSP/ESMFold). We hypothesize leakage is substantial and arises during NORMAL decoding rather than only under adversarial optimization, because the model re-encodes the concept through alternative features at later positions/denoising steps. We further hypothesize leakage is predicted by concept redundancy - the effective rank of the concept subspace, pre-specified and shown to predict beyond property frequency, SAE sparsity, and classifier confidence - and validate a redundancy-aware fix that clamps the concept subspace rather than a single feature, on held-out properties and models. We report leakage rates, a redundancy-based reliability predictor, and the validity/diversity cost of subspace clamping. Results turn feature interventions from an assumed-safe knob into an auditable, quantifiable one for safe scientific design.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Models (both frozen): (a) a GPT-style autoregressive SMILES chemical LM (~10M, trained on a ChEMBL/ZINC subset, or a public checkpoint) with a TopK SAE (k=32, dictionary 16,384) on the residual stream at a mid layer; (b) ESM-2 150M/650M (masked protein LM) with a residual-stream TopK SAE. SAEs trained on 20M activation-tokens (500k-sequence/molecule subset), Adam lr 1e-3, batch 4,096, 3 SAE seeds. Undesired properties (concrete, with HARD model-independent evaluators): molecules - specific PAINS/toxicophore substructures (e.g., nitro/aromatic-amine toxicophore), a reactive Michael-acceptor group, or exceeding a ring/heteroatom bound (RDKit SMARTS); proteins - a specific catalytic/binding motif such as the Ser-His-Asp triad (HMMER/regex) and a disallowed secondary-structure target such as a forbidden beta-sheet content (DSSP on ESMFold). For each property, the single best encoding feature and the ranked set of features above a concept-correlation floor (the candidate concept subspace) are recorded via concept-correlation and probe AUROC on held-out objects. REDUNDANCY METRIC (pre-specified before results): effective rank of the concept subspace = participation ratio of the singular values from SVD of the correlated-feature activation matrix on held-out objects; reported alongside, but claimed distinct from, raw feature count and SAE reconstruction error. "Clamp" = fixing the feature to a strong suppressive value at every decoding step. Generation seeds: 5.

Experiment 1 (H1 - feature suppression leaks in the finished object): Tests whether clamping the best feature still lets the property appear in finished objects at rates single-forward-pass evidence would deem impossible. Falsifiable primary endpoint (fixed decoding settings, intervention strength, and property class): the forward-pass-vs-end-object gap = (Leakage Rate) minus (the residual property rate implied by the clamp's single-step logit/probe suppression), where Leakage Rate = fraction of FINISHED objects still containing the property under the hard evaluator despite the active clamp. Convincing result: gap >= 20 percentage points for at least half the target properties. Decision band: gap in [10, 20] points -> leakage present but modest; partial support. Negative result (gap < 10 points) means interventions are reliable - a valuable positive result about intervention fidelity, refuting the leak hypothesis. Data/systems: N = 2,000 objects per property, generated under conditions that naturally exhibit the property (property-biased sampling/seed contexts). Controls/baselines: (i) no intervention (baseline occurrence), (ii) the single-forward-pass 'success' estimate, (iii) random-feature clamp of matched activation magnitude, (iv) matched-capacity clamp (same number of directions, random). Robustness sweeps: clamp magnitude up to validity collapse, decoding temperature, and generation length. A re-routing trace on leaked objects (which alternative features carry high concept-probe activation where the property re-emerges) plus one-by-one ablation of those features confirming leakage drops identifies the leak paths.

Experiment 2 (H2 - redundancy predicts leakage): Tests that leakage is predictable from how redundantly the concept is encoded. Decisive metric: Spearman rho between per-property Leakage Rate and the pre-specified effective-rank redundancy score. Convincing result: redundancy rho >= 0.5 (CI excludes 0) while single-feature concept-correlation shows rho within [-0.2, 0.2]. Decision band: redundancy rho in [0.3, 0.5] -> suggestive. Negative result (redundancy no more predictive than concept-correlation) refutes H2. Crucial ablation: partial correlation showing redundancy predicts leakage BEYOND property base-frequency, SAE sparsity (k), and concept-classifier confidence. Data: tens of target properties per domain (many toxicophores/motifs) to power the regression, bootstrap CIs.

Experiment 3 (H3 - redundancy-aware suppression closes the leak): Tests that clamping the full concept subspace, not one feature, removes the leak. Decisive metric: Leakage Rate as a function of subspace dimension k (projecting out the top-k correlated directions). Convincing result: Leakage Rate falls monotonically with k and drops below 5% at modest k (k <= 8) while validity/diversity cost stays acceptable (RDKit-validity / pseudo-perplexity / ESMFold pLDDT within 10% of baseline, bounded off-target property drift, and generation diversity retained). Decision band: leakage reaches [5%, 15%] only at large k, or the k needed incurs cost beyond 10% -> the fix works at a price; report the leakage-validity frontier. Negative result (subspace clamping does not reduce leakage below single-feature clamping) undercuts the redundancy account. Generalization: the fix is validated on HELD-OUT properties and on a masked/diffusion generation setting to test whether iterative denoising leaks differently than autoregressive decoding.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Hard evaluators define the property crisply, but restricting to properties with unambiguous structural evaluators limits generality; fuzzy properties (e.g., 'developability') are out of scope. 2) Leakage could be an artifact of weak clamping; mitigated by sweeping clamp magnitude to validity collapse and reporting leakage across the range, plus random-feature and matched-capacity clamp controls. 3) SAE quality and layer choice may confound which features 'encode' the property; controlled with multiple SAE architectures/layers and probe-based verification. 4) In-silico validity and property calls (ESMFold, RDKit) are proxies for wet-lab truth; claims concern model-internal controllability and structural facts, not experimental function. 5) The redundancy predictor could be underpowered with few properties; mitigated by tens of properties per domain and partial-correlation controls for base-frequency, sparsity, and classifier confidence. 6) If leakage is negligible, that is still a valuable positive result establishing intervention reliability, and the redundancy analysis explains why.

Name: synthesizability_blindspot_steering
Title: The Synthesizability Tax: Does Interpretable-Feature Property-Steering Systematically Trade Manufacturability for Target Gains, and Is Synthesizability Itself a Steerable Direction?
