Convincing positive: invariant steering retains >= 80% of the controlled-oracle gain while cutting provenance-collapse by >= 30% and restoring novelty toward the unsteered baseline, AND the positive control recovers the planted shortcut (detection AUROC>=0.9) with the fix removing it. Decision band: controlled-gain retention in [60%, 80%) or collapse reduction in [10%, 30%) means the fix trades some genuine signal for debiasing -- reported as a quantified trade. Negative: invariant steering destroys controlled-oracle gain (retention < 60%) means physics and provenance are inseparable for that property (reported per property), or a failed positive control invalidates the pipeline and is reported before any real-data claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Provenance-controlled oracles and physics evaluators (FoldX/Rosetta, second logP model) are in-silico proxies; the core claim rests on DISAGREEMENT between a naive predictor and a provenance-decorrelated one, plus displacement into a provenance feature subspace—stated explicitly, not as wet-lab truth. 2) Physics and provenance may be irreducibly entangled for some properties (family IS the mechanism); we handle this by reporting the entanglement per property and restricting strong claims to properties where a provenance-orthogonal physics direction demonstrably exists (validated by the controlled oracle). 3) The debiasing fix could remove genuine signal if physics and provenance share a subspace; we quantify the tradeoff via the controlled oracle rather than assume a free lunch. 4) SAE quality/layer choice could produce spurious 'provenance features'; controlled with multiple SAE variants, difference-of-means baselines, random-direction controls, and the synthetic positive control (experiment 6). 5) If standard steering turns out NOT to ride provenance (gains survive the controlled oracle), that is a valuable positive result establishing that interpretable-feature steering targets physics, not database artifacts. 6) In-silico property/validity metrics limit conclusions to model-internal design behavior, not experimental function.

Name: kinetic_thermodynamic_steering_gap
Title: Steer the Endpoint, Not the Path: Do Interpretable Features Control Thermodynamic but Not Kinetic Properties of Generated Molecules?
Short Hypothesis: We make one primary, typed claim and one audit claim. (Primary phenomenon—an endpoint-vs-pathway controllability gap) Interpretable SAE features of molecular/protein generators trained on STATIC endpoints afford causal, steerable control over THERMODYNAMIC/equilibrium properties (stability, binding affinity, solubility, fold free energy) but NOT over KINETIC properties (transition-state barriers, folding rates, metastability, dissociation kinetics): steering toward a kinetic target silently shifts the thermodynamic ENDPOINT instead, a 'kinetics blind spot,' because pathways/barriers are absent from endpoint-only training. Kinetic control is scoped as decodable-but-weakly-steerable under tested interventions, not universally absent. (Audit) An intervention-free internal kinetic-consistency signal flags these silently-uncontrolled designs better than equilibrium-property checks. The general principle we test: dynamical/pathway controllability of a generator is contingent on dynamics-bearing training data, so endpoint checks can certify a design that is kinetically invalid.
Related Work: Two threads meet for the first time. (1) 'Physics Steering' (2025) shows a PHYSICS foundation model (trained directly on simulation trajectories) has causally-steerable directions for dynamical concepts like diffusion speed and temporal progression; Latent Thermodynamic Flows (2025), Thermodynamic Interpolation (2025), and tLaSDI (2024) build generative models that capture temperature/kinetics but do so by INJECTING thermodynamic structure or training on dynamics data. (2) Molecular/protein interpretability-of-generation (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; chemistry-LM SAEs 2025; Circuits/Features/Heuristics in Molecular Transformers 2025) discovers and steers features for endpoint/equilibrium properties and never touches kinetics. Crucially, the physics-FM result raises the sharp question: does a generator trained ONLY on static molecules/sequences (no trajectories, no barriers) also learn steerable dynamical/kinetic handles, or is dynamical controllability contingent on dynamics-bearing training data? No prior work (a) contrasts kinetic vs thermodynamic steerability in molecular/protein generators, (b) surfaces the kinetics-blind-spot phenomenon where kinetic steering collapses to endpoint change, or (c) audits when a generator's kinetic-property claim is trustworthy. This introduces the endpoint-vs-pathway axis into interpretability-of-generation, distinct from all my prior proposals (folding fold, symmetry, conservation, synthesizability, syntax) which concern static structural facts, not dynamical/pathway properties. Contrast of prior families (closest-baseline delta in the last row): [endpoint steering] InterPLM/ProtSAE/chemistry-LM SAEs—steer equilibrium properties, never kinetics; [dynamics-trained generators] Latent Thermodynamic Flows/Thermodynamic Interpolation/tLaSDI—capture kinetics by INJECTING dynamics or training on trajectories; [physics-FM trajectory steering] Physics Steering—steerable dynamical directions BUT the model is trained on simulation trajectories; [THIS proposal] a static-endpoint-trained generator with SAE steering, asking whether a kinetic handle exists WITHOUT dynamics-bearing training data. The precise delta from the closest baseline: static-trained SAE steering, not trajectory-trained dynamical steering. Novelty locus is a FINDING (an endpoint-vs-pathway controllability gap) plus an evaluation PRINCIPLE, not a new theory of kinetics. Who cares: molecular design (barrier-aware generation), protein engineering (folding-rate/off-rate design), and mechanistic interpretability (what dynamical structure static training can and cannot induce); in practice they would add pathway-aware checks and stop trusting endpoint-only steering for kinetic targets.
Abstract: A molecule's usefulness often depends on kinetics, not just thermodynamics: a metastable polymorph, a slow-off-rate binder, a fast-folding protein, or a low-barrier catalyst are defined by PATHWAYS and BARRIERS, not equilibrium endpoints. Generative models for molecules and proteins are trained almost entirely on static endpoints, yet interpretability-guided design increasingly steers their features to hit target properties. Our one primary, falsifiable claim is an endpoint-vs-pathway controllability gap: interpretable features causally control THERMODYNAMIC properties but not KINETIC ones, so steering toward a kinetic target silently shifts the thermodynamic ENDPOINT instead—a 'kinetics blind spot' invisible to equilibrium and validity checks. The strongest so-what: endpoint checks can certify a design that is kinetically invalid. Recent work shows a physics model trained on trajectories has steerable dynamical directions; we test the complementary hypothesis that generators trained WITHOUT dynamics lack a causal kinetic handle. Using ESM-2 protein LMs and a SMILES chemical LM with sparse autoencoders, plus cheap kinetic oracles (contact-order folding-rate proxies, ML-interatomic-potential barrier estimates, Langevin mean-first-passage-time) validated on a small higher-fidelity subset, we LOCATE thermodynamic and kinetic features, CAUSALLY contrast endpoint against pathway control with endpoint-matched pairs and randomized-label controls, quantify the blind spot, and AUDIT whether an internal kinetic-consistency signal flags silently-uncontrolled designs before expensive simulation. Concrete uses: slow-off-rate binders, folding-rate design, barrier-aware molecule generation. Either way is a general evaluation principle for generative design: a positive kinetic handle is a surprising capability; a null tells designers to add pathway-aware checks and not trust endpoint-only steering.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Models (FROZEN): ESM-2 (150M and 650M) for proteins (generation by masked infilling) and a GPT-style SMILES chemical LM (~15M params) for molecules. Only SAEs are trained: TopK and Ordered/Matryoshka SAEs (Ordered can recover steerability TopK's decodable-but-inert features lack), expansion 16x, k=32, 30M activations at an intrinsic-dimension-chosen layer, seeds 0/1/2. THERMODYNAMIC/endpoint oracles: protein fold stability (a fine-tuned stability head or FoldX-style dG), GRAVY, DSSP secondary-structure content on ESMFold; molecule logP/QED, solubility proxy. KINETIC/pathway oracles: protein folding-rate proxy from absolute contact order (the Plaxco relation) and a native-state metastability proxy; molecule reaction-barrier estimate via a pretrained ML interatomic potential (climbing-image NEB-lite on fixed reaction templates) and mean-first-passage-time from short Langevin dynamics. Because kinetic oracles are compute-heavier, they are run on a capped 2,000-object subset per level. Validity gates: ESMFold pLDDT + pseudo-perplexity (proteins), RDKit-validity + synthetic accessibility (molecules). Data: for calibration, ~52 two-state proteins from a folding-kinetics database (e.g., ACPro/KineticDB) plus a fixed set of reaction templates; first confirm the frozen models natively span a meaningful kinetic RANGE (so absence-of-control is meaningful). Steering = add alpha*d_hat; alpha over {0,1,2,4,8}.

Experiment 1 (H1 - thermodynamic/equilibrium features are causally steerable): Identify thermodynamic features (correlate with stability/logP endpoints; probe AUROC/R^2) and steer toward a target endpoint. Systems: SAE-feature steering vs random-direction control. Decisive metric FIRST: on-target endpoint effect size (Cohen's d, steered vs unsteered, at the within-validity-budget alpha). Decision band: d >= 0.8 AND >= 0.4 over random control for >=2/3 of features => thermodynamic control genuine (H1 holds); d over control in [0.2,0.4) => inconclusive; < 0.2 => not steerable (premise fails).

Experiment 2 (H2 - kinetics is decodable-but-weakly-steerable, and steering a kinetic target silently changes the thermodynamic endpoint instead): (a) DECODABILITY: partial-correlation probe for the kinetic property controlling for the endpoint; report R^2 (low R^2 here is itself consistent with kinetics being absent from static endpoint-only training). (b) STEERABILITY: steer the best candidate kinetic direction (SAE feature, difference-of-means fast-vs-slow, activation-patching, endpoint-orthogonalized direction) toward a kinetic target while holding the endpoint fixed. Decisive metrics FIRST: (i) LEAKAGE FRACTION = share of steering displacement landing on the endpoint axis rather than the kinetic axis; (ii) SILENT-KINETIC-FAILURE RATE = fraction of 'kinetically-steered', valid objects whose kinetic property did not move beyond oracle noise (or moved wrong-sign) while an endpoint changed; (iii) ratio r = kinetic efficacy / thermodynamic efficacy from Experiment 1. Decision band: r <= 0.33 AND leakage >= 0.60 AND silent-failure >= 0.30 => kinetics blind spot confirmed; r in (0.33,0.67) or leakage in (0.40,0.60) => partial (test Ordered SAEs); r >= 0.67 => a genuine kinetic handle exists in a static-trained generator, refuting H2 (surprising, equally reportable).

Experiment 3 (H3 - the blind spot is invisible to equilibrium checks but an internal kinetic-consistency signal flags it): (a) INVISIBILITY: Spearman rho between endpoint-property change / pseudo-perplexity and true kinetic change; band |rho| <= 0.20 => equilibrium checks miss it, |rho| >= 0.40 => they catch it. (b) INTERNAL FLAG: a no-intervention score = kinetic-probe confidence / SAE-feature coherence read mid-generation; Decisive metric FIRST: AUROC detecting the silently-uncontrolled designs from Experiment 2 vs output-side signals (endpoint property, validity, likelihood). Decision band: internal AUROC >= 0.75 AND >= 0.10 over the best output-side detector => flag confirmed; margin (0.05,0.10) => inconclusive; margin <= 0.05 => no better (reported honestly). ROBUSTNESS & SCALE: both domains, two ESM-2 sizes, TopK vs Ordered SAEs; test whether kinetic steerability rises with model scale - no rise is consistent with the 'absent from training signal' explanation; a finding counts where stable on >=2 axes.

PRE-REGISTERED DECISION (blind spot vs no-evidence). 'Kinetics blind spot' is asserted ONLY if (a) the frozen model natively spans a kinetic range AND (b) thermodynamic control is calibrated (Exp 1 passes) AND (c) kinetic efficacy r <= 0.33 with leakage >= 0.60; if (a) or (b) fails we report 'no evidence / uninterpretable,' not a blind spot. OPERATIONAL, DOMAIN-SEPARATED PROPERTY DEFINITIONS (no bundling): proteins—thermodynamic = fold stability dG and DSSP secondary-structure content; kinetic = folding rate (contact-order/Plaxco proxy) and native-state metastability; molecules—thermodynamic = logP/QED/solubility proxy; kinetic = reaction-barrier height (ML-interatomic-potential NEB-lite on fixed templates) and mean-first-passage-time (short Langevin). Each property gets its own probe, direction, and decision band.

ADDED CONTROLS: (i) endpoint-matched pairs (same thermodynamic endpoint, different kinetics) to isolate endpoint-independent kinetic signal; (ii) randomized kinetic-label controls (shuffle kinetic targets) to bound spurious efficacy; (iii) oracle-noise sensitivity (repeat with injected proxy noise; require conclusions stable). STRONGER BASELINES beyond SAE features: random directions, endpoint-orthogonal directions, raw-activation linear probes/edits, and a black-box no-SAE steering baseline (optimize a raw-residual direction). HIGHER-FIDELITY VALIDATION: on a small subset, corroborate barrier proxies with short metadynamics/xTB and folding-rate proxies with literature two-state rates; strong claims restricted to where fidelity tiers agree.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Kinetic properties are assessed by in-silico proxies (contact-order folding-rate predictors, ML-interatomic-potential barrier estimates, short-Langevin MFPT), which are approximations of true kinetics and far cheaper than full MD; we validate proxies against each other and against literature rate data on a subset, and restrict strong claims to cases where proxies agree. Claims concern model-internal, proxy-verified kinetic controllability, not experimental rates - stated explicitly. 2) The kinetic-non-steerability claim is partly an ABSENCE claim; we mitigate by trying multiple intervention types (SAE features, difference-of-means, activation patching, endpoint-orthogonalized directions), sweeping strength, requiring the model to natively span a kinetic range, and head-to-head calibrating that THERMODYNAMIC features ARE steerable in the same pipeline - so a null kinetic result is meaningful rather than a weak-model artifact. A positive result (a genuine steerable kinetic handle in a static-trained generator) is equally publishable and surprising. 3) Kinetics and thermodynamics are partly coupled (Bell-Evans-style barrier-stability correlations); the partial-correlation feature selection and endpoint-matched dissociation pairs (step 5) are designed to isolate genuinely endpoint-independent kinetic signal, and we report where separation is impossible. 4) Kinetic oracles (NEB/Langevin) are compute-heavier than endpoint oracles; we cap simulation on a subset and use the internal audit precisely to reduce this cost. 5) SAE quality/layer choice could confound Location; controlled with TopK and Ordered SAEs, multiple layers, raw-activation probes, and random-direction controls. 6) An internal kinetic probe might not beat a black-box raw-activation probe on raw AUROC; the interpretability diagnosis (thermodynamics-decodable-and-steerable, kinetics-decodable-but-weakly-steerable) and the audit/compute-saving payoff remain the contributions, reported honestly. 7) If kinetic steering unexpectedly succeeds, it overturns the hypothesis but yields a strong positive finding that static-trained generators encode causal pathway information.

Name: steering_sideeffect_law
Title: The Conservation of Trouble: Are Off-Target Property Drifts of Interpretable-Feature Steering Lawful and Predictable in Scientific Generative Models?
Short Hypothesis: When an interpretable feature is steered to control one property of a generated protein or molecule, it induces off-target drift in OTHER, structurally-verifiable properties that is not random noise but LAWFUL: the drift vector across all properties is predicted, before any generation, by a fixed feature-specific 'side-effect signature' derived from the geometry of the SAE dictionary. This lets practitioners forecast and pre-empt collateral damage, choosing minimal-side-effect features and orthogonalized directions to hit a target property while holding others fixed.
Related Work: Text-LLM steering studies extensively document off-target side effects and entanglement: SAE-Targeted Steering (Chalnev et al. 2024) minimizes side effects using SAE-measured effect vectors; Rogue Scalpel (2025), Steering Externalities (2026), SteeringSafety (2025), Steering Refusal with SAEs (2024), and Mind the Performance Gap (2026) all show steering degrades unrelated capabilities or safety in a method/model-dependent way. Crucially, all of these (a) operate in TEXT LLMs where the off-target 'property' is a fuzzy behavior or benchmark score, and (b) treat side effects as a nuisance to be measured post hoc or empirically minimized. Scientific-model steering work (InterPLM 2024, ProtSAE 2025, chemistry-LM SAEs) reports only ON-target property gains and evaluates validity as a side constraint, never characterizing structured off-target property drift. No prior work (i) transfers the off-target-drift phenomenon to scientific generative models where every off-target property (helix content, charge, logP, ring count, motif presence) is an OBJECTIVELY VERIFIABLE structural fact, (ii) tests whether the drift is LAWFUL and predictable a priori from a fixed feature side-effect signature rather than needing per-target measurement, or (iii) turns that law into a pre-flight side-effect forecaster and a minimal-collateral feature/direction selector. This distinguishes it from my prior compositionality proposal (which co-steers several INTENDED targets) by studying UNINTENDED drift on non-targeted properties and its a-priori predictability. DELTA vs text-LLM pre-intervention side-effect prediction (Chalnev et al. 2024, SAE-Targeted Steering): they minimize side effects using effect vectors MEASURED empirically per target, whereas we predict the drift vector A PRIORI from fixed dictionary geometry (decoder overlaps + property-Jacobian) with NO generation, against HARD structural oracles. We claim a domain- and battery-specific empirical regularity, not a universal theory. Three separable contributions: (1) the finding (structured drift), (2) the predictor (geometry-derived signature), (3) the method (minimal-collateral controller); each is publishable on its own even if a later one fails.
Abstract: Steering an interpretable feature to control one property of a generated protein or molecule is the standard controllable-design paradigm, judged mainly by whether the target property moves. In text language models, steering is known to cause off-target effects, and SAE-based methods (e.g., Chalnev et al. 2024) minimize them using EMPIRICALLY-MEASURED effect vectors; but there the off-target 'property' is a fuzzy behavior and the effect must be measured per target. We make two moves. First, a new SETTING: in scientific generative models every off-target property (helix content, charge, logP, ring count, motif presence) is an objectively verifiable structural fact, so collateral drift becomes a measurable VECTOR, not a benchmark wobble. Second, a sharper QUESTION: can that drift be predicted a priori, before any generation, from the SAE dictionary geometry alone? We hypothesize each feature carries a fixed 'side-effect signature' -- computable from decoder-direction overlaps and a per-feature property-Jacobian -- that forecasts its drift vector. We frame this as a domain- and battery-specific empirical regularity, not a universal law. Using ESM-2 and a SMILES chemical LM with sparse autoencoders, we test three separable hypotheses: (1) single-target steering induces structured, non-random off-target drift under hard oracles; (2) the geometry-derived signature predicts each feature's measured drift vector, with a NO-SURROGATE decoder-overlap-only variant guarding against proxy leakage; and (3) the signature powers a pre-flight forecaster and a minimal-collateral controller (low-drift feature selection or orthogonalization) that hold non-target properties fixed, quantifying compute saved versus generation-based screening. Users and workflows: protein design, molecular optimization, and multi-property/constraint-satisfaction generative design, plus model evaluation and safety auditing of steered outputs.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Models: ESM-2 at 150M and 650M parameters and a GPT-style SMILES chemical LM (~90M), base weights frozen. SAEs: TopK (k=32, dictionary 16384) and Matryoshka on the mid-layer (60% depth) residual stream, trained on 200M activations, seeds {0,1}, FVU reported. Property battery, each with a cheap HARD oracle so drift is objective: proteins -- alpha-helix fraction, beta-sheet fraction, GRAVY, net charge, molecular weight, motif presence (HMMER/regex); molecules -- logP, QED, ring/aromatic-ring count, molecular weight, TPSA, functional-group SMARTS. Validity gates: ESMFold pLDDT>=0.6 + pseudo-perplexity within 1.5x baseline (proteins); RDKit-validity + SA<=6 (molecules). Feature bank: ~30-50 property-linked target features per domain (probe AUROC>=0.8 on 2,000 held-out natural objects) plus difference-of-means directions. Steering budget in normalized activation-norm units; norm-matched random-direction controls throughout; 500 generations per feature x strength level. SCOPE: the side-effect signature is computed PER FEATURE and predicts a drift VECTOR over the full property battery; we test whether it holds per model size, per SAE variant, and per domain, and report where it fails rather than asserting universality. All decisive thresholds below are reported with bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Single-target steering induces structured, non-random off-target drift). Tests that steering one property drifts other properties in a consistent, non-noise direction. Data/systems: for each target feature, sweep steering strength {0.1...1.0}; at each level measure the FULL property vector; the off-target drift vector = change in every non-target property; compare against a norm-matched random direction. Decisive metrics: (a) collateral magnitude = off-target drift norm relative to on-target gain; (b) DIRECTION CONSISTENCY = mean cosine of the drift vector across seeds and adjacent strengths; (c) correlation of output-side checks (validity/pseudo-perplexity/RDKit-validity) with true off-target drift. Convincing positive: direction consistency >= 0.7 (drift is a stable signature, well above the random-direction control's ~0) AND output-side-vs-drift correlation in [-0.2, 0.2] (standard evals are blind to it). Decision band: consistency in [0.4, 0.7) means drift is partly structured, partly noise -- reported as such; output-side correlation with |r| in (0.2, 0.4] means checks catch some drift, tempering the blind-spot claim. Negative: consistency < 0.4 (drift is essentially random across seeds) refutes H1's "lawful" premise -- a clean negative result warning against a-priori side-effect claims.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- A geometry-derived side-effect signature predicts the drift vector). Tests that an intervention-free signature computed from the SAE dictionary forecasts each feature's measured drift vector. Data/model: per feature compute (i) decoder-direction overlaps -- cosine of the feature's decoder direction with other property features' directions; (ii) a per-feature property-Jacobian -- gradient of each differentiable-surrogate property predictor w.r.t. residual-stream activations projected onto the feature direction. Predict the drift vector from these; correlate with the measured drift vector from Experiment 1; baselines -- concept-correlation and a chance permutation. Decisive metric (primary): cosine similarity / R^2 between predicted and actual drift vectors across features, plus per-property Spearman. Convincing positive: predicted-vs-actual drift cosine >= 0.6 (bootstrap CI excludes the concept-correlation baseline and chance) -- establishing lawfulness. Decision band: cosine in [0.35, 0.6) means the signature captures the dominant coupling but misses structure -- reported as partial law, usable for ranking not exact forecasting. Negative: cosine <= 0.35 (no better than concept-correlation/chance) means the drift is not predictable from dictionary geometry, refuting H2 (H1 may still hold descriptively).

Experiment 3 (H3 -- Pre-flight forecaster ranks features by collateral before generation). Tests that the signature ranks features by expected total collateral without any generation. Data/systems: use the signature to rank all target features by forecast total collateral for each target property; validate against the measured collateral from Experiment 1. Decisive metric: precision@k for selecting genuinely low-collateral features, and rank correlation (Spearman) between forecast and measured collateral. Convincing positive: precision@5 >= 0.8 and Spearman >= 0.6 (CI excludes 0), with quantified compute saved vs generation-based screening, plus a human-readable forecast per feature. Decision band: precision@5 in [0.6, 0.8) or Spearman in [0.4, 0.6) means the forecaster is a useful but imperfect screen -- reported with its error rate. Negative: precision@5 <= 0.6 means the ranking is not actionable, and the forecasting payoff is withdrawn.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- Minimal-collateral controller hits target while holding others fixed; positive control). Tests that selecting low-forecast-collateral features or orthogonalizing against held-fixed property axes Pareto-dominates naive steering. Data/systems: (a) select lowest-forecast-collateral feature for the target; (b) orthogonalize the steering direction against the property-Jacobian axes of properties to be held fixed; compare to naive best-concept-correlation steering on on-target gain, off-target drift on held-fixed properties, validity, novelty. POSITIVE CONTROL: two features constructed to share a decoder subspace (high overlap) and two known-orthogonal ones -- confirm the signature predicts high vs low cross-property drift. Decisive metric (primary): area of the target-gain-vs-collateral Pareto frontier, and held-fixed drift reduction at matched on-target gain. Convincing positive: orthogonalized/selected steering cuts held-fixed drift by >= 30% at matched on-target gain (Pareto-dominates naive), AND the positive control shows high-overlap pairs drift >= 3x more than orthogonal pairs. Decision band: held-fixed drift reduction in [10%, 30%), or on-target gain lost to achieve it, is a quantified trade rather than domination -- reported as such. Negative: no frontier improvement over naive steering (< 10% drift reduction), or a failed positive control, means the controller offers no practical collateral control and the applied claim fails.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) In-silico property oracles (ESMFold/DSSP, RDKit/SMARTS, biopython) are proxies for wet-lab truth; claims concern model-internal, structurally-defined off-target drift and its predictability, not experimental function. 2) The property-Jacobian requires a differentiable surrogate for properties measured by non-differentiable evaluators (HMMER motifs, folding); we quantify surrogate fidelity and also report the purely-geometric decoder-overlap predictor which needs no surrogate. 3) Off-target drift could be dominated by generic validity collapse rather than structured coupling; we isolate the regime where objects stay valid and report structured drift separately, using random-direction controls. 4) The law may be property-pair- or model-specific rather than universal; we test multiple properties, model sizes, and SAE variants and report where it fails—a negative/conditional result is still informative. 5) The orthogonalization fix may reduce on-target gain or interpretability; we quantify the tradeoff on the frontier rather than assume a free lunch. 6) SAE quality/layer choice could confound both drift and signature; controlled via multiple SAE variants, layers, difference-of-means baselines, and the positive control. 7) If drift turns out to be unpredictable noise, that is a clean, publishable negative result constraining theories of feature-dictionary geometry and warning against a-priori side-effect claims.

Name: shared_concept_causal_bridge
Title: One Knob, Two Worlds: Do Proteins and Molecules Share Causally-Steerable Physicochemical Concepts in a Unified Sparse Autoencoder?
Short Hypothesis: Novelty boundary against shared-dictionary SAEs (USAE/SPARC/JSAE): the claim is not merely that a protein language model and a small-molecule language model share latent features, but that a SMALL set of well-grounded physicochemical concepts (hydrophobicity, charge, aromaticity, molecular size, polarity) is carried by SHARED interpretable directions that are CAUSALLY USABLE for bidirectional generation control—clamping one shared feature simultaneously and monotonically shifts the corresponding property in BOTH modalities' generations. We further hypothesize shared features are more causally steerable and validity-preserving than modality-private features encoding the same concept. We treat cross-modal feature HETEROGENEITY (a split dictionary) as a live contingency the study may find rather than an established sharing hypothesis: a low sharing rate is a reported, informative outcome, not a failure.
Related Work: Two threads meet here but have never been combined for causal generative control across scientific object types. (1) Cross-model/cross-modal SAEs—USAE (2025), SPARC (2025), and group-sparse multimodal SAEs (2026)—learn shared concept dictionaries across vision/language models, and 'Beyond Converging Representations' (2025) shows scientific foundation models across string/graph/3D/protein modalities are representationally aligned and collapse when extrapolating. (2) Single-modality scientific SAE steering—InterPLM (2024), the chemistry-LM SAE (2025), Matryoshka SAEs on ESM2-3B (2025), CB-pLM (2024)—discovers and steers interpretable features WITHIN one model of one object type. Crucially: (a) all cross-modal SAE work is descriptive/retrieval-focused and never tests CAUSAL steering of generation; (b) all scientific steering work is confined to a single object type and never asks whether a concept has a single unified causal handle across proteins AND molecules. MolBind (2024) and protein-GDM alignment (2024) align modalities via contrastive learning but do not extract interpretable, individually-steerable, causally-validated shared features. We are the first to (i) train a unified SAE bridging a protein LM and a molecule LM, (ii) identify shared physicochemical concept features, and (iii) test whether ONE shared feature causally steers the SAME property in both modalities' generations—turning cross-modal interpretability from a similarity metric into a shared design lever. That closest negative finding—cross-modal representations align but collapse under extrapolation, and multimodal SAEs often learn split dictionaries—sets our null. We argue proteins and molecules may nonetheless share more transferable directions than vision-language pairs because both are governed by the SAME underlying physicochemical axes (hydrophobicity, charge, aromaticity), a shared physical basis absent between pixels and text; whether that yields shared CAUSAL handles is exactly what we test.
Abstract: Physicochemical concepts—hydrophobicity, charge, aromaticity, molecular size, polarity—govern both proteins and small molecules, yet generative models for each are studied in isolation and steered by modality-specific machinery. We ask whether a single interpretable 'knob' controls the same property across worlds. Building on cross-model sparse autoencoders (USAE, SPARC), we train a unified SAE that jointly reconstructs the residual-stream activations of a protein language model (ESM-2) and a SMILES molecule language model, encouraging shared latents via cross-reconstruction and global sparsity. We identify SHARED features—dimensions active on a common concept in both modalities—versus modality-private ones. Our central test is causal: clamp a single shared feature and measure whether it simultaneously and monotonically shifts the property in BOTH protein generations (GRAVY, net charge, aromatic content) and molecule generations (logP, formal charge, aromatic-ring count), while preserving validity. A pre-registered success criterion defines 'shared' by thresholded concept agreement in both modalities, a minimum causal effect size, and correct cross-modal monotonicity on predefined property probes; we compare against independent SAEs, random shared features, matched private features, and per-modality difference-of-means, and ablate whether cross-reconstruction is necessary versus a simpler group-sparsity objective. If it holds, the payoff is a shared latent interface for cross-modal property control—transferring a validated concept-knob between lead optimization and protein redesign, and enabling cross-modal model debugging—plus mechanistic evidence for a modality-invariant physical abstraction in scientific foundation models. If sharing is low, we report which concepts resist unification, a clear and informative bound on cross-object conceptual structure.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Protein side (frozen): ESM-2 150M/650M; molecule side (frozen): a GPT-style SMILES chemistry LM (~10M, ChEMBL-trained). Residual-stream activations at a mid layer (intrinsic-dimension-elbow) collected for a large protein corpus (500k-sequence UniRef sample) and molecule corpus (500k-molecule ChEMBL/ZINC sample); no paired protein-molecule data is used - alignment is concept-level via the shared objective. Unified SAE: a joint TopK / global-TopK SAE (k=32, dictionary 16,384) ingesting either modality with modality-specific encoder/decoder heads and a cross-reconstruction term (USAE/SPARC-style); a group-sparse variant for robustness; 3 SAE seeds. Baseline: two independent per-modality SAEs. Per-modality reconstruction fidelity and the fraction of cross-modally active latents (dictionary sharing rate) reported. Concept set {hydrophobicity, net charge, aromaticity, molecular size, polarity} with per-modality evaluators: proteins - GRAVY, net charge at pH7, aromatic-residue fraction, molecular weight, a polarity index (Biopython); molecules - RDKit logP, formal/partial charge, aromatic-ring count, MW, TPSA. Generation: masked infilling / activation-conditioned decoding (proteins), activation-steered autoregressive decoding (SMILES); 5 seeds. Pre-registration: the 5 concepts, their property evaluators, validity gates, layer choices, and statistical tests are fixed before causal measurement, and 'shared' requires passing the pre-declared concept-agreement, effect-size, and cross-modal monotonicity thresholds. An explicit ablation compares the cross-reconstruction objective against a plain shared/group-sparsity objective to test whether cross-reconstruction is necessary for shared causal handles.

Experiment 1 (H1 - shared concept directions exist in the joint SAE): Tests whether physicochemical concepts are carried by single latents active and property-correlated in BOTH modalities. Decisive metric: number of the 5 concepts admitting a SHARED feature (high concept-correlation in both modalities), and the sharing rate versus the independent-SAE baseline (which cannot produce shared indices). Convincing result: >= 3 of 5 concepts admit a shared feature, at a sharing rate above a co-labeling chance control. Decision band: 2 of 5 concepts shared -> partial sharing; report which concepts resist sharing. Negative result (<= 1 of 5, i.e. a split dictionary) refutes H1 but informatively bounds cross-modal abstraction. Matched modality-PRIVATE features (equally high correlation in only one modality) are recorded for Experiment 3.

Experiment 2 (H2 - one knob controls the property in both worlds): Tests whether clamping a single shared feature causally moves the property in each modality's generations. Decisive metric: bidirectional causal success rate = fraction of shared features that produce a significant, correctly-signed property shift in BOTH modalities. Convincing result: bidirectional causal success >= 0.5, exceeding random-direction and unrelated-feature controls, with consistent sign/monotonicity across modalities and validity retained (ESMFold pLDDT, pseudo-perplexity; RDKit-validity, SA). Decision band: bidirectional success in [0.3, 0.5] -> some shared knobs work; report which concepts. Negative result (< 0.3 or not above controls) means co-labeling did not imply a unified causal handle, refuting H2. Data: each shared feature clamped over a swept range, 200 objects per modality per setting.

Experiment 3 (H3 - shared features beat modality-private ones): Tests whether shared features are more steerable and validity-preserving than private features encoding the same concept. Decisive metric: control-validity Pareto frontier area for (i) the shared feature, (ii) the best matched modality-private feature, (iii) per-modality difference-of-means directions, per concept. Convincing result: the shared feature's frontier area is >= the best private feature's at equal validity for a majority of concepts, with better cross-modal steering-sign consistency. Decision band: shared within +-10% of private frontier area -> parity, not superiority; report as "shared no worse." Negative result (shared clearly below private) refutes H3. Supporting analyses: cross-modal steerability Spearman rho (does a shared feature's steerability in one modality predict the other; genuine handle if rho >= 0.5) and a transfer demo (validate a concept knob once on the cheap molecule model, apply the same shared feature to steer protein generation, report fraction of native effect recovered). Robustness across two protein sizes, two SAE variants, and layer choices.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) In-silico property evaluators and validity metrics (ESMFold, RDKit) are proxies for wet-lab truth; claims concern model-internal, cross-modal controllability, not experimental viability. 2) The joint SAE may learn a 'split dictionary' where most features stay modality-private (the known failure mode from multimodal SAE work); we mitigate with global-TopK and group-sparse objectives and report sharing rate honestly—a low sharing rate is itself an informative result about the limits of cross-modal abstraction. 3) A feature co-labeled as shared could reflect coincidental concept-correlation rather than a unified causal handle; the bidirectional causal test and cross-modal steerability-prediction analysis are designed to distinguish these. 4) Proteins and molecules have very different tokenizations and activation statistics, which may make joint reconstruction hard; we control by comparing to independent per-modality SAEs and reporting per-modality reconstruction fidelity. 5) Steering the molecule LM and masked/infilling protein generation are different decoding regimes; we standardize property measurement on finished objects and use random-direction controls to ensure comparability. 6) Layer/strength choices could confound sharing and steerability; we sweep strength within the validity budget and test multiple layers and SAE variants.

Name: steerability_emergence_pretraining
Title: When Does a Design Lever Get Forged? Tracing the Pretraining Emergence of Causal Feature Steerability in Protein Language Models
Short Hypothesis: In protein language models, the causal STEERABILITY of an interpretable feature (its ability to control the corresponding property in generation) emerges LATER in pretraining than its DECODABILITY (linear readout of the concept), and the emergence time of both is gated by the training-data frequency of the underlying biological concept: rare-but-valid concepts become decodable long before—or without ever—becoming steerable. This decodability-steerability lag is a training-time phenomenon that explains the widely-reported 'decodable-but-inert' anomaly and predicts which design levers a given checkpoint can and cannot provide.
Related Work: Two literatures converge but have never met. (1) Feature-emergence-during-pretraining work is entirely in TEXT LLMs: 'Evolution of Concepts in Language Model Pre-Training' (2025) and 'Crosscoding Through Time' (2025) use crosscoders to track feature formation; 'The Birth of Knowledge' (2025) maps categorical feature emergence across time/space/scale; and most relevantly 'How Does Controllability Emerge in LMs During Pretraining' (2025) shows linear STEERABILITY of text concepts emerges at intermediate stages and varies by concept, linked to linear separability. None studies scientific generative models, none ties emergence to training-DATA-FREQUENCY of the concept, and none contrasts decodability vs causal steerability trajectories for GENERATED scientific objects. (2) Protein-SAE work (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; 'From Mechanistic Interpretability to Mechanistic Biology' 2025; automated neuron labelling 2025; motif-gated causal patching 2025) is entirely inference-time on a FINAL checkpoint, and reports the 'decodable-but-inert' anomaly as a static puzzle. Data-scaling/bias work (Scaling and Data Saturation in pLMs 2025; pLMs biased by unequal sequence sampling 2024; Compute-Optimal pLMs 2024) shows data frequency shapes likelihoods but never connects it to feature steerability. We are the first to (i) trace decodability AND causal steerability trajectories across pretraining in a scientific generative model, (ii) test data-frequency as the gating variable via curated rare/common concepts and yearly-snapshot corpora, and (iii) reframe the decodable-but-inert anomaly as a training-time developmental lag with a predictive rule for checkpoint-conditional controllability. This uses Formation Tracing—a genuinely different mechanism strategy from prior inference-time steering studies. Our contribution is two-fold and separable: (a) the PHENOMENON—a decodability-then-steerability developmental lag gated by concept training-frequency; (b) the MEASUREMENT PIPELINE—checkpoint-wise SAE + causal steering + frequency-controlled onset estimation. Null-novelty is well-defined: if the lag is already established in text LMs, the protein-specific frequency-gating and the decodable-but-inert reconciliation remain the delta; if the lag appears in neither text nor protein models, that null itself constrains explanations of the anomaly to non-temporal causes.
Abstract: Interpretability-guided design assumes that if a concept is decodable from a protein language model it can be used as a design lever—yet multiple studies report 'decodable-but-inert' features that read out a concept perfectly but fail to steer generation. We propose that this anomaly is a developmental one: during pretraining, the causal STEERABILITY of a feature emerges strictly later than its DECODABILITY, and both are gated by how frequently the underlying biological concept appears in the training data. We test this by pretraining small ESM-style masked protein LMs (3.5M–35M params, tractable for an academic lab) and saving frequent checkpoints, complemented by publicly available yearly UniRef-snapshot pLMs. At each checkpoint we train a sparse autoencoder and, for a curated bank of concepts spanning a wide data-frequency range (common folds/motifs to rare families and rare property combinations), we measure two trajectories: decodability (probe AUROC of the concept feature) and steerability (causal property change per unit steer in generation, verified by DSSP/ESMFold/HMMER). We hypothesize (i) a consistent decodability-then-steerability ordering with a measurable lag, (ii) that concept training-frequency predicts both onset times, and (iii) that some rare concepts remain decodable-but-inert at convergence—explaining the static anomaly. We further test whether an emergent 'steerability onset' at one scale predicts onset at another, and whether upsampling a rare concept in a controlled retraining accelerates its steerability onset. Results would recast steerability as a trainable, data-dependent developmental property and yield a decision rule for practitioners and scaling researchers: a frequency-and-cheap-checkpoint predictor of which design levers a checkpoint can safely provide—when a decodable concept is usable for control and when it is not.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP (used by all experiments below). Models: masked protein LMs in the ESM-2 family at three scales, 3.5M, 8M, and 35M parameters, trained from scratch by us on a fixed 20M-sequence random subset of UniRef50 (UniRef50 has ~60M clusters; we use 20M to keep one 8M/35M run inside a single-GPU-week on one A100-40GB). All weights trainable during pretraining; frozen at each checkpoint for probing/steering. Key hyperparameters: masking rate 15%, batch 2048 sequences, max length 256, LR 4e-4 cosine with 2k warmup, AdamW, ~1.0e10 tokens total; we save 18 checkpoints log-spaced in tokens (10^7 ... 10^10). Three pretraining seeds {0,1,2} per scale for the 3.5M and 8M models, one seed for 35M (budget). Independent data-frequency axis: the four public yearly UniRef-snapshot ESM checkpoints where released. SAE: one TopK SAE (k=32, dictionary 8192, trained 100M activations, seed 0) per checkpoint on the mid-layer residual stream (layer at 60% depth), reconstruction FVU reported; a raw-activation linear probe is the SAE-independent decodability control, and a difference-of-means (SAE-free) steering direction is the SAE-independent steerability control. Inter-checkpoint SAE feature-matching (activation-correlation / Hungarian matching across adjacent checkpoints) and per-checkpoint reconstruction FVU are reported so that measured emergence timing reflects feature FORMATION rather than feature reallocation. For every concept we record confound covariates—concept complexity (evaluator/description length), sequence conservation, motif length, Pfam family size, and corpus redundancy—for use in Experiment 2. Concept bank: 40 concepts with hard automated evaluators and exact training-corpus frequency (counted in our 20M subset): 12 common (alpha-helix and beta-sheet fraction via DSSP on ESMFold, GRAVY hydrophobicity, molecular weight, zinc-finger and catalytic-triad motifs via HMMER/PROSITE), 28 deliberately rare (rare Pfam families with 50-500 corpus hits, uncommon motifs, and rare property combinations such as high-beta + high-hydrophilicity). DECODABILITY(concept, checkpoint) = held-out probe AUROC of the best SAE feature (and raw-activation probe) on 2,000 natural sequences. STEERABILITY(concept, checkpoint) = property change per unit steering norm during masked-infilling generation at the largest strength that keeps validity (pseudo-perplexity within 1.5x of unsteered and ESMFold pLDDT >= 0.6*baseline), verified by the concept's own evaluator over 500 generations, with random-direction and unrelated-feature (non-concept) controls subtracted to establish specificity.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Decodability emerges before steerability: the lag). Tests that within a concept, DECODABILITY crosses its detection threshold at an earlier training-token count than STEERABILITY. Data: the 40-concept bank above, evaluated at all 18 checkpoints x 3 scales. Systems compared, per concept: decodability trajectory vs steerability trajectory across checkpoints. Define onset = first checkpoint at which a trajectory crosses a fixed threshold (decodability AUROC >= 0.75; steerability >= 2x the matched random-direction control effect and property change >= 0.5 SD of the natural-sequence property distribution). Decisive metric: paired difference lag = log10(steerability-onset tokens) - log10(decodability-onset tokens), aggregated over concepts (Wilcoxon signed-rank, Hedges g). Convincing positive: median lag >= 0.3 log10-tokens (i.e. steerability onset at >= 2x the tokens of decodability onset) with signed-rank p < 0.01 in >= 2 of 3 scales. Decision band: median lag in [0.1, 0.3) log10-tokens is INDECISIVE given our 18-checkpoint spacing (a lag below the ~0.13-log10 gap between adjacent checkpoints cannot be resolved); we then densify checkpoints x2 around detected onsets before concluding. Negative result: median lag <= 0 (steerability never later than decodability) refutes the developmental-lag account and is reported as such, constraining explanations of the decodable-but-inert anomaly to non-temporal causes.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- Concept training-frequency gates both onsets, correlational). Tests that higher corpus frequency predicts earlier decodability-onset and steerability-onset, and that steerability-onset is the more frequency-sensitive of the two. Data: the same onsets from Experiment 1 paired with each concept's exact corpus frequency (range 50 to ~2M hits across the 40 concepts). Model: mixed-effects regression of log10(onset tokens) on log10(frequency), random intercept per scale and per concept-family. Decisive metric: standardized slope beta_freq for each onset type and the contrast beta_steer - beta_decode. Convincing positive: beta_freq significantly negative for both (higher frequency -> earlier onset) with steerability strictly more sensitive, |beta_steer| - |beta_decode| >= 0.15 (95% bootstrap CI excludes 0). Decision band: contrast in [0.05, 0.15) means frequency gates onset but the differential sensitivity is UNRESOLVED at n=40 concepts; we report the main frequency effect and flag the contrast as underpowered rather than claim asymmetric gating. Negative: beta_freq CI includes 0 means frequency does not gate onset, sending the causal test (Experiment 3) to adjudicate whether a confound (concept complexity, conservation) drives the null.

Experiment 3 (H2 -- Upsampling a rare concept causally accelerates its steerability-onset). Tests the gating claim causally by manipulating frequency alone. Data/model: retrain the 3.5M model (cheapest, 3 seeds) with 6 chosen rare concepts upsampled 10x versus a matched control run, total tokens held fixed at 1.0e10 so only relative frequency changes. Systems compared: upsampled vs control run, on the 6 treated concepts and 6 untreated rare controls. Decisive metric: shift in steerability-onset (log10 tokens) for treated concepts, upsampled minus control, paired across seeds. Convincing positive: treated concepts advance their steerability-onset by >= 0.3 log10-tokens (95% CI excludes 0) while untreated controls shift by < 0.1 log10-tokens. Decision band: treated advance in [0.1, 0.3) log10-tokens is a WEAK causal effect; we report it as directional support insufficient to claim frequency is the dominant lever. Negative: treated shift indistinguishable from control (< 0.1) means frequency is not the causal gate, overriding any correlational signal from Experiment 2.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- The lag explains decodable-but-inert and predicts a checkpoint's usable levers). Tests that concepts which are decodable-but-inert at convergence are exactly those whose steerability-onset never crosses threshold, and that this is predictable cheaply. Data: convergence checkpoint (10^10 tokens) of all three scales; plus cross-scale onset ordering from all checkpoints. Systems compared: (a) per concept at convergence, decodable-but-inert label (AUROC >= 0.75 AND steerability < threshold) vs the frequency-plus-small-model-onset predictor; (b) steerability-onset ordering at 3.5M vs at 35M. Decisive metrics: (a) fraction of the 40 concepts that are decodable-but-inert at convergence, and AUROC of predicting that label from {log-frequency, 3.5M steerability-onset}; (b) Spearman rho between 3.5M and 35M steerability-onset ranks. Convincing positive: a non-trivial inert fraction (point estimate reported with Wilson CI) with predictor AUROC >= 0.80, and cross-scale rho >= 0.6 (p < 0.01), giving a cheap-model rule for which levers a target checkpoint provides. Decision band: predictor AUROC in [0.65, 0.80) or rho in [0.4, 0.6) means the anomaly is real but only partially predictable; we ship the predictor with its measured error rather than as a guarantee. Negative: inert fraction ~0 (no concept is decodable-but-inert at convergence) means the static anomaly does not reproduce in our models and the explanatory claim is withdrawn; AUROC ~0.5 or rho ~0 means the lag is not predictable and offers no practical lever-forecasting rule.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Small self-trained pLMs may underperform large models, so absolute steerability could be weak; we mitigate by focusing on RELATIVE trajectories/orderings and by cross-checking with public yearly-snapshot pLMs. 2) SAE quality varies across checkpoints and could confound emergence timing; we control with a fixed SAE architecture/hyperparameters per checkpoint, report reconstruction fidelity, and cross-validate decodability with an SAE-independent raw-activation probe. 3) In-silico evaluators (ESMFold, DSSP, HMMER) are proxies for wet-lab truth; claims concern model-internal, training-time controllability, not experimental viability. 4) Frequency-onset correlations could reflect confounds (concept complexity, sequence conservation) rather than raw frequency; the controlled upsampling retraining (Experiment 3) is designed to isolate frequency causally. 5) Checkpoint spacing may miss sharp emergence transitions; we use log-spaced checkpoints and can densify around detected transitions. 6) If decodability and steerability emerge simultaneously (no lag), that is still an informative, publishable result refuting the developmental-lag account and constraining explanations of the decodable-but-inert anomaly. 7) Retraining runs add compute cost but are limited to the smallest models to stay within an academic budget. 8) Concept-bank selection could bias results; the bank is constructed by a pre-registered procedure (fixed evaluators, exact corpus-frequency binning into 12 common / 28 rare concepts, hard automated labels) reported in full so selection bias and reproducibility can be assessed.

Name: steering_fails_on_memorized_designs
Title: You Can't Steer a Memory: Interpretable-Feature Control Silently Fails on Memorized Scientific Designs
Short Hypothesis: Scientific generative models occupy a hybrid regime that memorizes some outputs (near-verbatim training retrievals) and generalizes others. We hypothesize that interpretable-feature steering, the dominant paradigm for controllable design, CAUSALLY FAILS on memorized generations while succeeding on generalized ones—because memorized objects sit at contractive attractors whose internal representations are 'spiky' and resist perturbation. Consequently, a cheap, intervention-free representation-spikiness score predicts, before any steering, whether a given generation is controllable, and steering evaluated only on aggregate averages hides a large, systematically uncontrollable memorized subpopulation.
Related Work: Two lines converge here for the first time. (1) Memorization geometry: 'Generalization of Diffusion Models Arises with a Balanced Representation Space' (2025) proves memorized samples yield spiky representations and are NOT steerable while generalized samples are steerable in representation space; 'Overparameterized autoencoders implement associative memory' (2018/2020) shows memorized examples are contractive attractors. (2) Scientific-model controllability: InterPLM (2024), ProtSAE (2025), and chemistry-LM SAE steering demonstrate interpretable features steer protein/molecule generation, but ALWAYS report AGGREGATE property gains and never partition outputs by memorization status. Meanwhile 'Transformer Learning in Sequence-Based Drug Design Depends on Compound Memorization' (2026) and protein-LM data-leakage studies (2024/2025) show scientific generative models are heavily memorization-driven, yet treat this as a benchmark-inflation problem, not a controllability problem. No prior work (a) tests whether the memorized-not-steerable geometry transfers to SCIENTIFIC generative models where memorization is objectively measurable via sequence identity to the training set, (b) shows interpretable-feature steering causally fails on the memorized subpopulation, or (c) validates a pre-flight spikiness score that predicts per-generation controllability. This distinguishes the proposal from all my prior steering-focused ideas (which assumed the target is steerable) and from the memorization literature (which ignores controllable design). Our PRIMARY contribution is a transferable cross-modal PHENOMENON—memorized-not-steerable geometry reappearing in scientific sequence models—plus a new per-generation OPERATIONAL definition of controllability; the intervention-free spikiness predictor is a secondary, practical by-product. This is a new evaluation STANDARD, not merely a mechanistic curiosity: it tells design teams, IP/safety auditors, and controllability researchers to partition steering metrics by memorization status, to pre-flight-filter which generations are controllable, and to audit the memorized subpopulation before trusting an aggregate property gain.
Abstract: Interpretable-feature steering has become the standard tool for controllable design of proteins and molecules, and it is universally evaluated by average property gains across many generations. We ask whether that average conceals a systematic failure mode. Recent geometry work shows generative models occupy a hybrid regime—memorizing some outputs as contractive attractors with 'spiky' internal representations while generalizing others—and that memorized samples resist representation-space steering. Scientific generative models are known to be heavily memorization-driven, and, uniquely, memorization here is objectively measurable: a generation is memorized if it is near-identical to a training sequence. We hypothesize that interpretable-feature steering is systematically far less effective on memorized generations than on generalized ones, so aggregate steering metrics hide a large, poorly-controllable subpopulation, and we quantify how often aggregate benchmarks mislead. Using ESM-style protein language models and a SMILES chemical language model with sparse autoencoders, we label each generation as memorized or generalized via sequence/structure identity to the (known) training corpus, then measure per-generation steerability of feature interventions against cheap property oracles. We test three claims: (1) steering property-gain and validity are far lower on memorized than generalized generations at matched steering budget; (2) an intervention-free representation-spikiness score (activation standard deviation / SAE-feature concentration) predicts per-generation steerability before any intervention, enabling a pre-flight controllability filter; and (3) nudging generation away from memorized attractors (light noise/temperature or a 'de-spiking' repulsion from the nearest training neighbor) restores steerability, at a measurable novelty cost. Results would reveal a hidden, safety- and IP-relevant blind spot, change steering-evaluation protocol (report metrics split by memorization status), and provide a cheap pre-flight test for when steering can be trusted.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Generators with KNOWN training corpora so memorization is objectively measurable: a self-trained ESM-style masked protein LM at 8M and 35M parameters on a defined 10M-sequence UniRef50 subset (one seed each; base weights frozen after training), plus a public ProtGPT2 checkpoint with a documented training set; and a GPT-style SMILES chemical LM (~90M) trained by us on a defined ChEMBL/ZINC subset. SAEs: TopK (k=32, dictionary 16384) and Matryoshka on the mid-layer (60% depth) residual stream, trained on 200M activations, seeds {0,1}, FVU reported. Cheap property oracles: proteins -- alpha-helix/beta-sheet fraction (DSSP on ESMFold), GRAVY, molecular weight, motifs (HMMER/regex); molecules -- RDKit logP, QED, ring/aromatic counts, functional-group SMARTS. Validity gates: ESMFold pLDDT>=0.6 + pseudo-perplexity within 1.5x baseline (proteins); RDKit-validity + SA<=6 (molecules). Feature bank: property-linked SAE features (probe AUROC>=0.8 on 2,000 held-out natural objects) plus difference-of-means directions as a non-SAE baseline. Steering budget in normalized activation-norm units (as in the norm of the added vector / mean site activation norm). Per-generation STEERABILITY = target-property change per unit budget within the validity gate, with norm-matched random-direction control subtracted.

Experiment 1 (H4/H1 -- Memorization labels split a large corpus, and the aggregate average hides the split). Tests that a substantial memorized subpopulation exists and that reporting only the mean steering gain conceals it. Data: 20,000 unsteered generations per model. Labels: MEMORIZED if nearest-training-example identity is high -- proteins: sequence identity >= 90% (mmseqs2/BLAST), optionally TM-score corroborated; molecules: Morgan-fingerprint Tanimoto >= 0.9 or exact canonical-SMILES match; GENERALIZED if nearest identity is low (proteins <= 50%, molecules Tanimoto <= 0.4). Decisive metric: memorized fraction per model (Wilson CI) and its dependence on model size and sampling temperature; plus the bimodality (dip test) of the aggregate per-generation steering-gain distribution. Convincing positive: memorized fraction >= 10% for at least one model AND the aggregate steering-gain distribution is significantly bimodal (dip test p<0.01) once split by label. Decision band: memorized fraction in [3%, 10%) means the blind spot exists but is small -- reported as a minority subpopulation; dip-test p in [0.01, 0.05) is suggestive-only bimodality. Negative: memorized fraction < 3% across all models means no meaningful memorized subpopulation exists here and the aggregate-blind-spot claim (H4) does not apply to these models.

Experiment 2 (H1 -- Steering fails on memorized, succeeds on generalized). Tests the core causal-status contrast at matched budget. Data/systems: memorized vs generalized generations matched on baseline property value and sequence length (to remove confounds); apply feature steering and difference-of-means steering at a swept budget {0.1...1.0}; norm-matched random-direction control. Decisive metric (primary): steerability GAP = generalized minus memorized per-generation steerability, mixed-effects model with memorization status as key factor (effect size, 95% CI), plus the control-validity frontier area per subpopulation. Convincing positive: generalized steerability exceeds memorized by >= 0.5 SD of the per-generation steerability distribution (CI excludes 0) with the same ordering in >= 3 of the 4 models. Decision band: gap in [0.2, 0.5) SD is a REAL but modest effect -- reported as partial, not "causal failure"; the aggregate frontier likely still usable on memorized. Negative: gap <= 0.2 SD (memorized as steerable as generalized) is a clean negative result that the diffusion-model memorized-not-steerable geometry does NOT transfer to these sequence models, and H1 is withdrawn.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- Intervention-free spikiness predicts controllability pre-steer). Tests that a cheap representation-spikiness score forecasts per-generation steerability before any intervention, and does so at least as well as the expensive memorization label. Data: all labeled generations from Experiment 1. Spikiness scores at the intervention site: activation SD across dimensions; SAE-feature concentration (top-feature mass fraction / feature-vector entropy); local contractivity proxy (representation change under small input perturbation). Systems: spikiness vs concept-correlation vs the (expensive) memorization label as predictors of the measured steerability from Experiment 2. Decisive metric: Spearman rho and R^2 of spikiness-vs-steerability, and precision@k for selecting the top-k most steerable generations. Convincing positive: rho >= 0.5 (bootstrap CI excludes 0) AND precision@100 >= 0.8 AND spikiness matches or beats the memorization-label predictor -- a usable intervention-free pre-flight filter with quantified compute saved. Decision band: rho in [0.3, 0.5) or precision@100 in [0.6, 0.8) means spikiness is a weak screen -- reported with its measured error, not as a reliable gate. Negative: rho <= 0.3 means spikiness does not predict steerability and the pre-flight-filter claim fails, even if the H1/H2 phenomenon holds.

Experiment 4 (H2 -- The attractor mechanism: leaving the memorized attractor restores steerability). Tests causally that spikiness/contractive-attractor geometry, not merely the memorization label, is what blocks steering. Data/systems: on memorized generations, apply three de-attractor interventions before steering -- (a) mild temperature/nucleus widening, (b) initial-token/masked-position perturbation, (c) explicit "de-spiking" repulsion from the SAE-representation of the nearest training neighbor -- each vs an untreated memorized control. Decisive metric: steerability gain (post minus pre de-attractor) on memorized generations, paired; reported jointly with the NOVELTY cost (drop in nearest-training-neighbor identity) and validity cost. Convincing positive: de-spiking raises memorized steerability to within 0.2 SD of the generalized baseline (recovering >= 60% of the Experiment-2 gap) at a novelty cost that keeps outputs below the memorized identity threshold. Decision band: gap recovery in [30%, 60%) is partial causal support -- the attractor account is one contributor; recovery achievable only at novelty cost that itself de-memorizes the object is reported as confounded (spikiness and memorization not separable here). Negative: no steerability gain from any de-attractor intervention means the contractive-attractor mechanism is not what blocks steering, so H2 is unsupported even if H1 holds descriptively.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Requires knowing the training corpus to label memorization; we mitigate by self-training small models on defined subsets and using public checkpoints with documented training sets, and by using high-similarity thresholds that give conservative memorized labels. 2) In-silico oracles/validity (ESMFold, RDKit) are proxies for wet-lab function; claims concern model-internal controllability and design reliability, not experimental viability. 3) Lower steerability on memorized generations could be confounded by their baseline property values or length; we control via matched-pair comparison and mixed-effects modeling. 4) Spikiness might merely correlate with memorization rather than causing low steerability; Experiment 4 (de-spiking restores steerability) is the causal test that disentangles this. 5) SAE quality/layer choice could affect both spikiness and steerability; we control with multiple SAE variants, layers, and difference-of-means baselines. 6) The word "causal failure" is reserved for the case where the de-spiking intervention (Experiment 4) cleanly restores steerability; otherwise we report a memorization-status ASSOCIATION, not causation. If steering turns out equally effective on memorized generations, that is still a valuable, publishable negative result establishing that the diffusion-model memorized-not-steerable geometry does NOT transfer to scientific sequence models—constraining theories of memorization geometry across modalities. 7) The de-spiking restoration trades novelty for controllability; we quantify this frontier rather than assume a free lunch.

Name: steering_reliability_collapse
Title: Controlled but Unrepresentable: Does Interpretable-Feature Steering Push Scientific Generative Models Into Their Own Confidence Blind Spots?
Short Hypothesis: Interpretable-feature steering is judged almost entirely by whether a target-property predictor improves. We hypothesize a distinct, currently-unmeasured failure: steering an interpretable feature to control a property silently drags generation into regions where the model's OWN representation becomes unreliable (its embedding drifts toward random-like, low-information vectors), because steering displaces activations off the training manifold along directions the feature was never calibrated for -- so the apparent property gain is least trustworthy exactly where steering is strongest, even when the finished object is valid and satisfies the predictor. We further hypothesize that a cheap, intervention-free, pre-registered representation-reliability score declines monotonically with steering strength beyond what a matched-OOD-but-unsteered control explains, predicts per-generation whether the claimed property is real versus illusory, and can gate steering to keep only trustworthy designs -- an axis existing property-predictor-plus-validity evaluation misses.
Related Work: Two threads meet for the first time. (1) SAE/neuron steering of scientific generative models (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; FoldSAE 2025; Automated Neuron Labelling 2025; Steering PLMs/ASPO 2025; ProtoMech 2026; antibody SAE 2025) all report property GAIN from steering and evaluate success via property predictors; none asks whether steering pushes outputs into regions where the model can no longer reliably represent them. (2) Representation-reliability work—'Quantifying Uncertainty in Protein Representations Across Models and Tasks' (2025) shows pLM embeddings for undersampled sequences become vector-indistinguishable from random, and 'Quantifying Feature Space Universality' plus data-saturation studies show embedding quality tracks training coverage—but this is studied only for NATURAL inputs, never as a CONSEQUENCE of steering, and never linked to the trustworthiness of controlled designs. No prior work (a) shows steering induces representation-reliability collapse, (b) demonstrates that property predictors and validity checks fail to detect this while an internal reliability score does, or (c) uses reliability to gate steering. This is distinct from my prior proposals on memorization-attractors (about contractive attractors resisting steering), validity-foresight (about invalid finished objects), and infeasible-spec frustration (about contradictory constraints): here the finished object can be perfectly valid and hit the property predictor, yet sit in a representational blind spot that makes the control claim untrustworthy. DELTA. The reliability/OOD literature ('Quantifying Uncertainty in Protein Representations' 2025) studies degraded embeddings for naturally undersampled inputs; our contribution is that STEERING actively INDUCES this collapse and ties it to the trustworthiness of controlled designs -- a steering-induced, not input-given, effect, separated from generic distribution shift by a matched-OOD-but-unsteered control. Primary novelty is the phenomenon; the pre-registered reliability score and the gating controller are secondary.
Abstract: Interpretable-feature steering is the dominant tool for controllable design of proteins and molecules, and it is judged almost entirely by whether a target-property predictor says the property increased. Our single novel claim is a phenomenon: steering causes the model's representation reliability to collapse in otherwise-valid outputs. The act of steering pushes generation into regions where the model's own embedding becomes unreliable -- drifting toward random-like, low-information vectors -- so the property 'gain' is measured on objects the model can no longer faithfully represent. Because such objects still fold, still parse, and still satisfy an external predictor, standard evaluation misses this. We hypothesize this arises because steering displaces activations off the training manifold; to separate a genuine steering effect from ordinary distribution shift we compare against matched-OOD-but-unsteered sequences. We pre-register a representation-reliability score with three components (distance-to-random, perturbation self-consistency, SAE-feature coherence) and test that it (1) declines monotonically with steering strength beyond the matched-OOD control; (2) predicts per-generation whether a property gain is real (agrees with an independent oracle) versus illusory; (3) beats output-side validity and predictor-confidence at flagging untrustworthy control, with thresholds fixed on a held-out set; and (4) gates steering to recover a trustworthy control-validity-reliability frontier. The result adds representational reliability as a missing evaluation axis: after this work, reporting steering success from property-predictor gain and validity alone is insufficient. The axis is relevant to any controlled generative-science workflow and would be adopted first by binder and molecule design teams shipping steered candidates to expensive validation.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Models: ESM-2 at 150M and 650M parameters and a GPT-style SMILES chemical LM (~90M), base weights frozen. SAEs: TopK (k=32, dictionary 16384) and Matryoshka on the mid-layer (60% depth) residual stream, trained on 200M activations, seeds {0,1}, FVU reported. Feature bank of 20-40 property-linked features (probe AUROC>=0.8 on 2,000 held-out natural objects): proteins -- alpha-helix/beta-sheet fraction, GRAVY, molecular weight, a thermostability proxy head, motifs; molecules -- logP, QED, ring/aromatic counts, functional groups. Property predictors used the way the steering literature uses them (DSSP/ESMFold, biopython, fine-tuned heads, RDKit/SMARTS). Validity gates: ESMFold pLDDT>=0.6 + pseudo-perplexity within 1.5x baseline (proteins); RDKit-validity + SA<=6 (molecules). Steering budget in normalized activation-norm units; SAE-feature, difference-of-means, and norm-matched random-direction interventions. REPRESENTATION-RELIABILITY SCORE (intervention-free), combining: (a) distance-to-random -- Mahalanobis/cosine gap between the object's embedding and the distribution of embeddings of shuffled/random sequences; (b) embedding self-consistency under small input perturbations (masking/dropout); (c) SAE-feature coherence (co-firing consistency vs natural objects); validated on natural held-out objects to track known coverage/neighbor-density signals before any steering use; each component (distance-to-random, perturbation stability, SAE-coherence) is reported individually as an ablation as well as combined, and both the combination weights and the reliability-gate threshold are fixed on a held-out calibration set only, never on test.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Steering pushes representations toward unreliable regions; H2 -- monotone collapse with strength). Tests that the reliability score declines monotonically with steering strength, often before validity or property-predictor gain break down. Data/systems: for each feature/property, sweep steering strength {0...1.0 budget units}; at each level generate 500 objects and record property-predictor gain, validity, and reliability score; compare SAE-feature, difference-of-means, and random-direction steering, and -- critically -- a MATCHED-OOD-BUT-UNSTEERED control (natural sequences sampled to match the off-manifold distance induced by steering, with no intervention) so a reliability drop attributable to steering can be separated from generic distribution shift. Decisive metric (primary): slope of reliability vs steering strength (mixed-effects), and the COLLAPSE-BEFORE-VALIDITY GAP = steering strength at which reliability crosses the natural-object 5th-percentile threshold minus the strength at which validity fails. Convincing positive: reliability slope significantly negative and monotone (Spearman rho <= -0.7 vs strength) with a positive collapse-before-validity gap >= 0.2 budget units in the majority of properties, and a steering-induced reliability drop exceeding the matched-OOD-but-unsteered control by >= 0.2 SD (isolating steering from generic distribution shift). Decision band: gap in [0, 0.2) budget units means reliability and validity collapse together -- the phenomenon exists but offers little early-warning headroom; reported as such. Negative: non-monotone or flat reliability (rho > -0.3), or a negative gap (validity fails first), refutes H1/H2 -- reliability collapse is not a distinct pre-validity failure mode, a clean negative result.

Experiment 2 (H3 -- Low reliability marks illusory property gains). Tests that the property "gain" is real when reliability is high and illusory when low, adjudicated by an independent oracle. Data/systems: for a subset of steered generations, score the target property with an INDEPENDENT oracle not used in steering (proteins: FoldX/Rosetta-style stability or a distinct structure metric; molecules: a second empirical logP model or docking); stratify by reliability quartile. Decisive metric (primary): predictor-vs-oracle agreement on the target property per reliability quartile (correlation or concordance). Convincing positive: agreement in the top reliability quartile exceeds the bottom quartile by >= 0.3 (correlation units), CI excludes 0 -- gains are trustworthy only when reliable. Decision band: quartile gap in [0.1, 0.3) means reliability weakly tracks trustworthiness -- reported as a soft signal, not a gate. Negative: gap <= 0.1 (predictor-oracle agreement independent of reliability) means the reliability score does not distinguish real from illusory gains, refuting H3 even if collapse (H1/H2) occurs.

Experiment 3 (H4 -- Output-side signals miss it; the internal score catches it). Tests that validity and property-predictor confidence are near-chance at flagging untrustworthy control while the internal reliability score succeeds. Data/systems: predict "low predictor-oracle agreement" (from Experiment 2) using the internal reliability score vs output-side baselines -- the predictor's own confidence, pseudo-perplexity, ESMFold pLDDT / RDKit-validity, and a black-box raw-activation reliability probe. Decisive metric: AUROC and calibration ECE for flagging untrustworthy generations. Convincing positive: reliability-score AUROC >= 0.80 with ECE<=0.10 while output-side validity/property-confidence stay in [0.45, 0.60] (near chance), the SAE score adding which-features-decohere interpretability. Decision band: reliability-score AUROC in [0.65, 0.80), or its edge over the black-box probe in [0.03, 0.10) AUROC, means the internal signal works but its advantage over cheaper signals is marginal -- the interpretability payoff is then the contribution. Negative: output-side signals already reach AUROC>=0.70, or the reliability score fails to beat them, means H4's "completely miss" claim is refuted.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- Reliability-gated steering keeps only trustworthy designs). Tests that gating steering by the reliability score yields a better trustworthy-yield-per-compute frontier than ungated or validity-only gating. Data/systems: a controller that rejects/down-weights steering driving reliability below the natural-object threshold, vs ungated steering and validity-only gating, over the same property battery.
